Ex Afreximbank President, Oramah urges Africa to turn global shocks into opportunities
items.description: By Henry Ojelu & Deborah Oladeji Former President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Professor Benedict Oramah, has urged African countries to take advantage of changing global realities and technological advancements to accelerate economic transformation. Oramah made the call while delivering the keynote address at the 20th AELEX Annual Lecture in Lagos, with the theme, “Beyond Survival: Global Shocks, the Information Age and Africa’s Opportunity to Leapfrog.” He said Africa must move beyond reacting to global disruptions and strategically position itself to benefit from emerging economic and technological opportunities. According to him, geopolitical tensions, deglobalisation and rising protectionism are reshaping the global economy, creating an opportunity for African countries to rethink their development strategies. He identified dependence on foreign capital, currencies and raw material exports as major constraints to the continent’s growth, stressing the need for African countries to take greater control of their resources and financial systems. “Capital is our greatest constraint. Capital that we own but do not control is not ours,” he said, noting that between $350 billion and $500 billion in African foreign exchange reserves were held outside the continent. Oramah called for the strengthening of indigenous financial institutions, increased local currency financing and investment in industries capable of processing the continent’s natural resources. He also advocated the expansion of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) and effective implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to boost intra-African trade. Citing Kenya’s mobile money revolution, he said technology could enable African countries to leapfrog traditional stages of development. He stressed the need for investment in energy infrastructure, data centres and critical minerals processing to prevent the continent from remaining dependent on technologies developed elsewhere. The Chairman of the occasion and Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria Limited, Mrs Bola Adesola, said effective leadership, strong institutions and adequate preparation were critical for businesses and governments to withstand global shocks. She emphasised investment in technology, business continuity planning and resilient supply chains, urging institutions to prepare for disruptions rather than wait for crises. In his welcome remarks, a founding partner of AELEX, Mr Fubara Anga, SAN, described the annual lecture as a platform for discussing national issues, influencing public policy and strengthening institutions. He called for greater involvement of state and local governments in attracting investments and driving economic development, rather than leaving the responsibility solely to the Federal Government. The question-and-answer session, moderated by Mr Femi Ojumu, examined issues including artificial intelligence, digital sovereignty and Nigeria’s energy infrastructure. items.title: Kwara converts Omu-Aran General Hospital to teaching hospital
items.description: By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin Kwara State Governor, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, on Wednesday laid the foundation for the conversion of the General Hospital, Omu-Aran, into the Thomas Adewumi University Teaching Hospital under a public-private partnership arrangement aimed at expanding access to specialised healthcare in Kwara South. The project is expected to strengthen medical education, improve healthcare manpower development and reduce the burden on existing tertiary health facilities in the state. Speaking at the foundation-laying ceremony, the governor, who was represented by his deputy, Kayode Alabi, described the initiative as a milestone in the development of healthcare infrastructure in Kwara South. “Today marks another milestone as we witness the establishment of the first Teaching Hospital in Kwara South. This remarkable achievement, conceived and actualised through a strategic partnership with the Kwara State Government through the Ministry of Health, will deeply promote medical education, improve human resources in health and contribute significantly to increasing access to quality healthcare delivery for our people,” he said. AbdulRazaq said establishing a tertiary healthcare facility in the southern part of the state would decentralise specialised medical services and reduce pressure on centrally located hospitals, which residents often find difficult to access. He expressed confidence that the facility would contribute to reducing preventable deaths and improving healthcare outcomes across communities. The governor said the project reflected his administration’s commitment to partnerships with private stakeholders to accelerate development, adding that upgrading the existing facility would bring medical services closer to residents of Omu-Aran and neighbouring communities. He commended the founder, management, staff and students of Thomas Adewumi University for their commitment to medical education and development, while urging residents of Omu-Aran to support the project. In his remarks, the Founder and Chancellor of Thomas Adewumi University, Engr. Johnson Bamidele Adewumi, said the former General Hospital, established on February 1, 1973, by the administration of the late General David Bamigboye, offered an opportunity to expand specialised healthcare services in Kwara South. He said the university adopted the teaching hospital project as part of its vision to train medical doctors and other allied health professionals. Adewumi explained that rather than establish an entirely new facility, the university approached the state government with a proposal to transform the existing hospital through a strategic partnership. He clarified that the arrangement did not involve the sale or transfer of ownership of the hospital. “Under the approved framework, ownership of the hospital remains firmly vested in the Government of Kwara State, while Thomas Adewumi University undertakes the construction and development of necessary academic infrastructure. For the avoidance of all doubt, the hospital was neither bought nor put on sale,” he said. The chancellor, however, appealed to the state government to provide the necessary financial support for the extensive upgrading of the hospital’s infrastructure and engagement of specialist consultants. He noted that the financial and technical requirements of a tertiary teaching hospital were beyond the capacity of a private individual or the host rural community. Adewumi said the project was designed to be completed within 18 months, adding that a team led by Professor Kuranga, a former Chief Medical Director of the University of Ilorin Teaching Hospital, and 17 other professors had been involved in developing the initiative. The ceremony was attended by government officials, traditional rulers and academics, including the Olupo of Ajase-Ipo, Oba Ismail Yahya Alebiosu; the Olomu of Omu-Aran, Oba Raheem Adeoti; the Commissioner for Health, Dr Amina Ahmed El-Imam; and a former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ilorin, Professor Shuaib Oba Abdulraheem. Also present were the APC senatorial candidate for Kwara South, Prince Lekan Adewoye, and Oloriewe Raheem Adedoyin, among other dignitaries. items.title: Nasarawa APC crisis: Govt calls for probe of rally disruption
items.description: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The Nasarawa State Government has called on security agencies to investigate an incident that reportedly disrupted activities surrounding Vice-President Kashim Shettima’s visit to the Emir of Lafia during Wednesday’s All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rally. The government made the call following reports of disturbances during the Vice-President’s visit to the traditional ruler and allegations of an incident involving Governor Abdullahi Sule at the rally held at Lafia Square. The governor’s Personal Assistant on Social Media, Emmanuel Innocent Akwe, had raised concerns over the incident, alleging that the governor was pelted with objects suspected to be stones by some aggrieved party members. In a statement, Akwe described the reported incident as unacceptable and called for respect for the office of the governor and the unity of the APC in the state. The state government subsequently expressed concern over the reported disruption of the Vice-President’s visit to the Emir, urging security agencies to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident. The Secretary to the State Government, Labaran Magaji, who made the government’s position known in a statement, said Shettima had visited the traditional ruler as a mark of respect for the traditional institution. He regretted that the visit was reportedly disrupted by actions he described as disrespectful to constituted authorities and the office of the Vice-President. Magaji urged security agencies to conduct a thorough investigation, identify those responsible for any wrongdoing and ensure that anyone found culpable was dealt with in accordance with the law. The development comes amid political disagreements within the state chapter of the APC following the party’s recent governorship primary. However, the circumstances surrounding the reported disturbances and the identities of those responsible have yet to be independently established. As of the time of filing this report, there had been no official clarification on the allegations surrounding the incidents. items.title: Orpailleurs burkinabè expulsés de Guinée : A Ouagadougou, les transporteurs se mobilisent aux côtés des autorités pour leur rapatriement
items.description: Environ 200 cars sont mobilisés à Ouagadougou pour rapatrier les compatriotes expulsés de Guinée. Si plusieurs cars ont bougé hier, une trentaine de cars étaient positionnés à la place de la Révolution, à Ouagadougou, ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026. Ces véhicules s'apprêtent à prendre la route pour aller chercher les Burkinabè expulsés des sites d'orpaillage en Guinée et faciliter leur retour au pays. Constat sur cette mobilisation. Depuis 2 heures du matin, ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, de nombreux cars appartenant à différentes compagnies de transport rallient la place de la Révolution, à Ouagadougou. Le ballet incessant des véhicules s'est poursuivi jusqu'à notre arrivée sur ce site de regroupement, d'où ils doivent prendre la direction de la frontière entre le Mali et la Guinée pour ramener nos compatriotes. À 11 heures, une trentaine de cars étaient déjà stationnés, en attente du départ. À leurs côtés, quelques convoyeurs piaffaient d'impatience à l'idée de partir à la rencontre de leurs compatriotes. « Nous sommes là depuis 2 heures du matin à la place de la Révolution pour aller à la recherche de nos frères », confie Moussa Zoromé, convoyeur à la Société de transport Ousmane et fils (STROF) International. En attendant le départ, ses confrères et lui prennent des clichés des véhicules et des différentes compagnies qui rallient progressivement le site. Moussa Zoromé, convoyeur à la Société de transport Ousmane et fils (STROF) International Antoine Kaboré, vice-président national de la Faîtière unique des transporteurs routiers du Burkina, est également à pied d'œuvre sous un soleil de plomb. Un calepin à la main, il enregistre chaque car qui rejoint le site. Pendant qu'il note le flux des véhicules, son téléphone ne cesse de sonner. « Ce sont des transporteurs qui veulent aussi envoyer des cars. Il y a un véritable engouement depuis hier », nous explique-t-il après avoir raccroché. La veille, confie-t-il, plus de quarante cars ont déjà pris la route. Une cinquantaine d'autres véhicules devraient également prendre le départ ce mercredi, ajoute-t-il. « Avec le gouvernement, les transporteurs se sont mobilisés comme un seul homme pour accompagner le président du Faso dans ses actions. Depuis que les événements se sont passés, on a senti un gouvernement au cœur de la population, qui travaille à ce que nos concitoyens rentrent avec dignité », fait-il savoir. Pour le vice-président national de la Faîtière unique des transporteurs routiers du Burkina, cette mobilisation dépasse les frontières de Ouagadougou. À Bobo-Dioulasso, deuxième grande ville du Burkina Faso, l'engouement est également au rendez-vous. L'objectif, souligne-t-il, est de préserver la dignité des Burkinabè partout où ils se trouvent. Selon lui, environ 200 cars ont été mobilisés depuis hier pour la cause. Deux heures après notre passage, soit à 14h, les cars avaient déjà bougé. Antoine Kaboré, vice-président national de la Faîtière unique des transporteurs routiers du Burkina, a salué la solidarité nationale autour de cette cause Des vivres également mobilisés Aux côtés des transporteurs, le ministère de l'Action humanitaire apporte également sa contribution à cette opération de solidarité. Sur le site de la place de la Révolution, de jeunes manutentionnaires déchargent un camion-benne rempli de sacs de riz. « C'est le ministère de l'Action humanitaire. Ce sont des vivres destinés à nos compatriotes qui arrivent. Le ministère veille toujours à ce que les gens puissent avoir de quoi manger », explique Antoine Kaboré. Lire aussi : Expulsion de Burkinabè de Guinée Conakry : Le gouvernement prend des mesures pour organiser leur retour dans « la dignité et la décence » Après la place de la Révolution, nous nous sommes rendus à la rencontre des responsables de certaines compagnies de transport. Mais les différents responsables n'ont pas souhaité s'exprimer. En effet, une délégation gouvernementale doit se rendre au Mali ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 afin d'apporter une assistance aux ressortissants burkinabè en situation de détresse et de faciliter leur retour au pays dans « la dignité et la décence ». Ces cars sont prêts pour le départ Face à cette situation, les autorités burkinabè ont appelé les populations au calme et à la retenue. Elles les ont également invitées à faire preuve de vigilance face aux tentatives de manipulation et de désinformation. Pour rappel, plusieurs ressortissants burkinabè pratiquant l'orpaillage artisanal sur le territoire guinéen ont été expulsés de ce pays. Serge Ika Ki Lefaso.net

items.title: IFC, Access Holdings partner to boost trade finance across Africa
items.description: .partnership targets businesses, cross-border trade, access to global markets By Udeme Akpan The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, and Access Holdings Plc have signed a partnership agreement to expand trade finance, support enterprise growth and improve African businesses’ access to regional and international markets. The partnership is expected to strengthen Access Group’s capacity to finance businesses, facilitate cross-border trade and support sustainable economic growth across its markets. The agreement, signed on the sidelines of the Africa Financial Industry Summit (AFIS) 2026 in Luanda, Angola, on November 4, 2026, also forms part of Access Holdings’ broader capital-raising programme aimed at attracting development finance institutions and other investors to support its growth. The agreement was signed by Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, Chairman, Access Holdings; Ethiopis Tafara, IFC Regional Vice President for Africa; and Roosevelt Ogbonna, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Access Bank Plc. Under the partnership, IFC’s investment is expected to reinforce the Group’s capital base, enabling it to sustain and expand financing for businesses and trade activities that drive economic growth across Africa. Commenting on the transaction, Aig-Imoukhuede said the partnership reflected a shared commitment to strengthening African financial institutions and supporting the continent’s economic development. He said: “Our partnership with IFC has always been anchored on a shared belief that strong African financial institutions are essential to Africa’s growth. This investment is a vote of confidence in the institution we have built and, in the direction, we are taking it. “Having built scale across Africa, our task now is to turn that scale into value: for the businesses we finance, the trade we facilitate and the communities we serve. “Strengthening Access Group’s capital base deepens its role as a bridge between Africa and global markets, enabling us to mobilise more trade finance and investment for African enterprises.” He added that the transaction was an important step in the Group’s efforts to attract long-term investment to support disciplined and sustainable growth. Also speaking, Tafara said expanding access to trade finance was critical to helping African businesses grow, enter new markets and create jobs. He said: “Across the World Bank Group, we are working to mobilize private capital, strengthen financial markets and create the conditions for private sector-led growth. “This partnership with Access Group will help channel more financing to businesses across the continent and translate Africa’s entrepreneurial potential into greater economic opportunity.” For IFC, the partnership aligns with its strategy of mobilising private capital and working with financial institutions to improve access to finance, strengthen markets and create opportunities for businesses to expand and generate employment. The post IFC, Access Holdings partner to boost trade finance across Africa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: LDC : Serhou Guirassy sort sur blessure et inquiète avant la double confrontation face à l’Érythrée
items.description: C'est probablement un coup dur pour la Guinée à quelques jours de sa double confrontation face à l’Érythrée. Serhou Guirassy a été contraint de quitter ses coéquipiers sur blessure, ce mercredi, lors de la rencontre entre le Borussia Dortmund et le Bétis Séville, comptant pour la phase de ligue de la Ligue des champions. Une situation qui suscite des inquiétudes quant à sa disponibilité pour les prochaines échéances du Syli national. Titulaire au coup d’envoi de cette rencontre européenne, l’attaquant international guinéen n’aura disputé que 34 minutes avant de céder sa place à la suite d’une blessure. Une sortie prématurée qui pourrait constituer un sérieux coup dur pour la sélection guinéenne, à l’approche de ses deux prochains rendez-vous internationaux. Pour l’heure, aucune communication officielle n’a été faite sur la nature exacte de la blessure de l’avant-centre du Borussia Dortmund, encore moins sur la durée de son éventuelle indisponibilité. Il est donc trop tôt pour se prononcer sur sa participation à la prochaine fenêtre internationale. Cette situation intervient à quelques jours de la double confrontation entre la Guinée et l’Érythrée, prévue les 12 et 16 novembre prochains, dans le cadre des 3e et 4e journées des éliminatoires de la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2027. Pièce maîtresse du dispositif offensif de Paulo Duarte, Serhou Guirassy représente l'un des atouts majeurs du Syli national dans cette campagne qualificative. Son éventuelle absence serait ainsi un handicap pour la sélection guinéenne, qui ambitionne de faire le plein de points face à l’Érythrée. Les prochaines heures devraient permettre d’en savoir plus sur la gravité de cette blessure et les chances de voir Guirassy répondre présent pour ces deux rencontres décisives. items.title: Dress code controversy hits Nigerian Law School over hijab ban during exams
items.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri Dress code is a serious matter at the Nigerian Law School, where students are expected to present themselves in a manner befitting the legal profession. However, the school’s dress policy has come under public scrutiny over alleged discriminatory treatment of Muslim candidates who wore the hijab to the ongoing Bar Final Examinations. The examinations, which began on October 31, are scheduled to end on November 7, 2026. The controversy stems from the school’s alleged refusal, particularly at its Bwari Campus in Abuja, to admit female candidates wearing long hijabs into the examination hall. Reports of hijab-wearing students in tears after being restricted by school authorities prompted a range of reactions from different interest groups While various Muslim groups insist that the hijab, which is already recognised under Part B, Rule 5 of the Nigerian Law School’s Code of Conduct for Students as acceptable attire for female students, must be retained even during examinations, the Association of Traditional Worshippers in Nigeria argues that its members should enjoy the same religious rights and be allowed to attend school activities in their traditional regalia, just as the hijab is permitted. Reacting to the development at the Law School, the Muslim Students’ Society of Nigeria (MSSN), B-Zone, in an open letter on the first day of the exams, condemned the reported restrictions on the hijab, describing them as discriminatory. It demanded an immediate review of the screening arrangements for candidates. The body argued that Muslim candidates should be allowed to participate in the examinations without being compelled to compromise their religious convictions. It argued that the wearing of the hijab is an expression of religious identity and should not be treated as an examination offence or an indication of academic misconduct. Referencing Sections 38 and 42 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, which guarantee freedom of thought, conscience and religion as well as protection against discrimination, the students’ group argued against subjecting candidates to unequal treatment because of their faith. Similarly, the Muslim Public Affairs Centre (MPAC) Nigeria, through its Executive Chairman, Disu Kamor, also flayed the reported treatment of hijab-wearing candidates, saying it had received complaints from the Bwari and Lagos campuses of the Law School. For its part, the Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) demanded a suspension of the examinations at all Nigerian Law School campuses over what it termed the harassment, intimidation and exclusion of female Muslim students wearing the hijab from examination halls. The Islamic human rights organisation, in a press statement issued by its Founder and Executive Director, Professor Ishaq Akintola, also demanded an investigation into the incidents. It vowed to mobilise parents, Muslim youths and other stakeholders for peaceful protests across Law School campuses nationwide if its demands were not met. “Hijabites who came hoping to sit for their call-to-bar final examinations were disallowed from entering the examination halls. “While this was going on, our office was inundated with telephone calls, text messages and chats. “We heard the cries of traumatised candidates, the lamentations of distressed parents hundreds of kilometres away from the examination centres and the agitation of concerned Muslims around the country. “MURIC strongly condemns the wanton disruption of the lawful educational pursuit of innocent Muslim ladies. It is crude, irrational and sadistic,” the body added. Meanwhile, the Law School has denied any form of discrimination or harassment of the female Muslim candidates who were screened for the examinations. The school, in a statement signed by its Secretary to Council and Director of Administration, A.O. Osho, said its examinations were conducted under established regulations designed to ensure proper identification, examination security and academic integrity. It disclosed that a female student wearing a hijab was recently apprehended after she was found with electronic devices concealed on her body. “On the 29th day of October 2026, a Bar Part I female student with her hijab on, was found with ear pod and a phone strapped to her thigh. “This incident is still being investigated under the school rules and extant regulations,” the school added, saying the incident reinforced the need for strict examination security measures. “The apprehension of the female student for examination malpractice during the Bar Part I examinations further underscores the necessity for strict and effective examination security measures. “Such measures, however, must be applied fairly and without discrimination,” the school stated, even as it pledged commitment to protecting the constitutional rights and religious freedoms of all students. It is worth noting that the intervention of critical stakeholders and the management of the school eventually led to an understanding that female Muslim students may wear only black, shoulder-length hijabs. This has, however, not gone down well with the Association of Traditional Worshippers in Nigeria, which insists that what is good for the goose should also be good for the gander. “Our position is founded on the inviolable principle of equality, religious freedom and non-discrimination. “If Muslim students are permitted to wear hijabs during examinations on the basis of religious convictions, then students who practise traditional African religions must equally be permitted to manifest their religious identities and convictions without discrimination, marginalisation or institutional hostility,” the group insisted. Remarkably, this is not the first time the hijab has sparked controversy over the dress code regulations for lawyers. On June 23, 2022, senior lawyer and activist, Chief Malcolm Omirhobo caused a stir at the Supreme Court by appearing for a hearing in native doctor regalia. Chief Omirhobo, who sauntered into the courtroom barefooted, wore his lawyer’s wig and black gown with a white shirt, though instead of black trousers and a suit, he wore a red wrapper with a mini-calabash amulet dangling from his neck. The lawyer, who also wore amulets on his wrist and ankle, sat comfortably in a row of chairs reserved for legal practitioners while proceedings of the apex court lasted. Although he was not accosted by security agents attached to the court, his bizarre appearance was not lost on a panel of justices of the Supreme Court, who quickly handled the case before them and retired to their chambers. Speaking to journalists after he exited the courtroom, Chief Omirhobo said his decision was based on a judgement the apex court had just delivered, which permitted the use of the hijab in public primary and secondary schools in Lagos. The Supreme Court, in a split decision of five to two justices, in an appeal marked SC/910/2016, which Lagos State, through its Attorney-General, filed against a minor, Miss Ayisat Abdukareem, and others, validated the use of the hijab in public schools. Chief Omirhobo insisted the verdict enforced his right to include his traditional regalia, being his mode of worship, in what he wore to the court. “You can see that I am not wearing shoes. Ifa has told me that if I wear shoes I’ll be dead. So I had no option; I had to obey the spirit. “You see this eye (pointing at the calabash amulet on his chest), without it I can’t see the evil spirit coming to attack me. So with this I can see them,” Chief Omirhobo told journalists, referencing the Supreme Court judgment. The case of Amasa Firdaus in 2017, when her hijab became the subject of controversy at the Call to Bar ceremony, also remains fresh in the memory. Amasa’s refusal to remove her hijab led the Council of Legal Education to withdraw her from the list of those to be admitted into the Bar. However, following high-level intervention, she was admitted into the Bar the following year. The latest hijab controversy may be settled, but traditional worshippers’ push for similar accommodation will likely keep the issue alive. The post Dress code controversy hits Nigerian Law School over hijab ban during exams appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: NACCIMA honours NAFDAC DG, hails war on fake drugs
items.description: …Adeyeye highlights reforms to boost industry, protect public health By Daniel Kudayah The Director-General of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC), Prof. Mojisola Christianah Adeyeye, has received an Award of Excellent Performance from the Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA) in recognition of her contributions to industrial growth and the fight against fake and substandard drugs. The award was presented at NACCIMA’s Breakfast Roundtable Meeting held at Providence Hotel, Lagos, where Adeyeye served as guest speaker. The meeting brought together members of the association, captains of industry and key stakeholders from the organised private sector to discuss regulatory processes, business growth and public health protection. In her keynote address, Adeyeye highlighted regulatory reforms introduced under her leadership, emphasising NAFDAC’s commitment to transparent, science-driven and business-friendly regulation. She explained that the agency’s regulatory framework was designed to support industrial growth while ensuring that only safe, quality and wholesome products reach Nigerian consumers. Industry leaders and other participants at the meeting commended the NAFDAC boss for her leadership, particularly her efforts to combat fake and substandard drugs and her contributions to creating a more supportive regulatory environment for businesses. They praised her commitment to safeguarding public health while promoting the growth and development of industries in Nigeria. The award, according to NACCIMA, recognised Adeyeye’s outstanding performance, hard work and contributions to industry and the fight against counterfeit and substandard products. The presentation was greeted with applause from participants at the event. NAFDAC, under Adeyeye’s leadership, has continued to pursue measures aimed at strengthening the regulation of food, drugs and other regulated products, with the dual objective of protecting consumers and supporting legitimate businesses. The recognition by NACCIMA underscores the importance of collaboration between regulators and the organised private sector in promoting product quality, consumer safety and sustainable industrial development. items.title: Bob Dylan Meets With Pope Leo
The Midwest Is Back on the Map for Democrats
items.description: L ast night, in the streets of Austin, Democrats honked their horns and hung out their windows, like it was V-E Day. In the nation’s capital, they blasted “Party in the U.S.A.” near the White House. But in southeast Iowa, the blue revolution came quietly. The Democrats of Des Moines County—a place that does not actually contain the state capital, but a small, industrial river city and rural areas along the Mississippi—have not come to associate Election Night with joy. The half dozen white-haired Iowans at the Burlington office’s “watch party” were blinking in disbelief at the TV as MS NOW election alerts flashed across the screen. Their party had retaken the governorship of Ohio—and somehow won a Senate seat in South Carolina? Texas was within reach. So, it seemed, was Kansas? “This might be a very big night,” Tom Courtney, a 79-year-old former state senator and former leader of the county party, told me, in what was already sounding like a colossal understatement. Iowa’s results had yet to come in. He and the other Democrats in the room seemed to be experiencing happiness only distantly, like birdsong from deep within a dark wood. This county, which had elected Barack Obama by about 23 points in 2008, was one of 31 Iowa counties that swung to Donald Trump in 2016. Two years ago, Trump won Des Moines County by 15 points, and Democrats began speaking of the “river counties” in the past tense—pieces of Iowa’s blue wall, lost forever. Courtney was on the phone. He paced the office, passing lawn signs, a cooling pot of chili, and the final slices of a Casey’s taco pizza. Then, suddenly, gasps. The countywide results were in, and a map of election results showed Des Moines County faintly—yet undeniably—blue. The county’s voters had opted to send a Democrat to the state house and another to the U.S. House; they’d also voted to make Rob Sand the state’s first Democratic governor elected in 20 years. “Did you hear that?” Courtney asked me, from across the room. By the end of the night, Iowa would also send Josh Turek to the Senate, plus three Democrats to the House. Kansas would send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since the invention of beer in a can. In Ohio, the party would send Sherrod Brown back to Congress, and Amy Acton to the governor’s mansion. At the office in Des Moines County, Courtney’s wife, Nancy, emerged from the office kitchen with several plastic cups full of room-temperature peppermint schnapps. “We did good,” she told the small group of people, which, despite the cavalcade of thrilling news, was maintaining a measured, midwestern composure. A fortunate combination of variables had put Iowa, and the rest of the Midwest, back on the map for Democrats. The next big challenge for the party will be keeping it there. W ar. Tariffs. Gas prices. It’s all I heard at the polls yesterday morning in Iowa, where, like pretty much everywhere else, the midterm elections were a referendum on choices made by President Trump. Even loyal Republicans I spoke with at the polls seemed bummed to be voting for the GOP. “Somebody’s gotta do it,” one man told me outside Burlington’s First Church of Nazarene when I asked how he felt about Republican leadership. Later, a woman on the other side of town told me she was eating mostly toast and tacos to save money. She’d still submitted an all-Republican ticket, she said. “But I didn’t want to vote for any of them.” Still, to have a night like last night, Democrats needed more than bad atmospheric conditions for Republicans: They needed good candidates. And where it mattered most, they had them. In Iowa, Democrats ran Sand, a centrist who has emphasized frugality and promised to take on corruption. “Right person, right message, right place, right time,” Sandy Dockendorff, a longtime Democratic activist in Des Moines County, told me. Her party also had Turek, a four-time U.S. Paralympian whose compelling backstory and commitment to moderation proved enough to defeat Ashley Hinson, widely considered to be the star Republican recruit of the cycle. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Jon Husted, despite the latter’s allegedly fantastic posterior . And in Kansas, Democrats managed to get Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who until recently was a Republican, at the top of the slate. It helped that Hamilton’s opponent, the incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, was impressively weak. “In a shitty environment, one way you don’t win races is to combine shitty candidates running shitty campaigns,” a senior—and very bitter—GOP strategist involved in multiple senate races, said. [ Read: Who thought this ad was a good idea? ] The lesson, according to national Democrats, is clear: The winning candidates were “comfortable being a different type of Democrat,” the party strategist Lis Smith told me in a text. Those candidates had worked hard to persuade independents and Republicans, even if “it didn’t always earn them fans online.” Perhaps Smith is referring, in part, to the way that Sand and Turek handled some of the most contentious issues facing the party. Both candidates, for example, ditched the party line to say that transgender girls should not play in girls sports. Last week, Turek released an ad about it that had sent many Democrats sputtering . He won anyway. “Democrats need to get better at winning rural voters,” Adam Jentleson, president of the center-left think tank Searchlight Institute, told me. “Iowa is the testing ground, and Sand and Turek are the models.” [ Read: The simple message that produced a Democratic landslide ] Last night, every county in both Kansas and Iowa moved left. Dockendorff, the longtime Des Moines County activist, had told me over coffee yesterday morning that something like this would happen. (I trusted her because, in 2020, she had been the Cassandra of the Caucuses, warning me —correctly—that Iowa’s vaunted nominating contest was likely to devolve into chaos.) “Iowa is turning back to purple,” she said. A year ago, or maybe less, Democratic activists had started filling chairs at county party meetings again. Some young people, too. Energy wise, she said, “there is no comparison to 2018.” This was much, much bigger. River towns, like Burlington, where the decline of unions had hollowed out the party, were showing some potential for Democrats once more. “I hear dissatisfaction from voters here,” she said. “People trusted Trump to do . He hasn’t done .” This assessment inspired another warning from Dockendorff—for Democrats both in and outside of Iowa. “This is not a coronation of the Democratic Party,” she said. It is an expression of frustration from voters looking for something different. “Our problem will be creating that something different.” Last night, for example, Iowans passed a constitutional amendment that will make it more difficult to raise income taxes, which might make it harder for Iowa’s new leaders to address the state’s budget shortfall. And voters in Des Moines County and others that flipped are not suddenly committed Democrats. National Democrats have been warning for months that a significant win in November would be over-interpreted by party activists and leaders, who would assume that voters were in love with their message, rather than simply sick of the president’s antics. The Democratic Party remains thoroughly unpopular. With Trump repudiated , albeit not totally in the rearview mirror, Democrats now have the challenge of presenting an affirmative vision for the country. How will they lower gas prices, or the price of milk? How will they talk about transgender issues as a party? Or immigration? Now, Dockendorff said, “the internecine war begins.” [ Read: The Democratic base is angry ] Signs of the coming conflict were on display last night at the watch party in Des Moines County. Sometime after the announcement that Florida Democrats had broken the state’s Republican supermajority but before the schnapps, Ben Diewold, a co-leader of the group, said he hoped that the Democrats wouldn’t try to impeach Trump again. “All that’s gonna do is invigorate MAGA,” he said. “Let Trump fade away.” Nancy didn’t agree. “He needs to be accountable to all that he’s done.” Soon, though, their conversation was interrupted. MS NOW was projecting that James Talarico had won in Texas. (“TalaFREAKO!” Diewold shouted.) And Rob Sand would lead Iowa. [ Read: How Texas turned blue ] “I’m glad I’m alive to see it,” Courtney said. He dictated a congratulations text and sent it to Sand. A few minutes later, a couple of the younger staffers, who’d come to work in Iowa from California and New Jersey, left to celebrate at a bar downtown. They asked Courtney to join them, but he declined. He wanted to keep watching. Madeleine Carlisle contributed reporting.

items.title: Google Puts a Price on Opting Out of AI in Schools
items.description: Over the past few years, Google’s low-priced laptops have become an AI Trojan horse in America’s schools. Students can use a school-issued Chromebook to automate much of their homework. Fire up the Gemini app, and Google’s chatbot will spit out a full essay about the meaning of The Giver . Type an algebra question into the Google search box, and an “AI Overview” will solve it for you. Ask a follow-up question, and the search box might give way to “AI Mode,” which turns the search engine into a full-on chatbot. Districts across the country give each student their own device, which typically comes equipped with a Google account and a suite of the company’s software. Over the past year, some of the country’s largest public-school districts, including Los Angeles and New York City, have passed policies limiting students’ screen time and banning generative-AI tools. But they hit an obstacle: Google didn’t offer schools a way to fully opt out of AI. Yesterday, the tech giant’s attempt to address the problem only made people madder. Google’s stand-alone Gemini chatbot will now be disabled by default for school accounts, the company announced . But Google quietly left out any option to turn off its most popular and widely used generative-AI features: those built into its search engine. In other words, the only way for schools to go AI-free is to cut off students’ access to Google Search, the world’s most popular website. Tech companies threatening to withdraw products rather than modify them has become part of Silicon Valley’s playbook. (Meta once responded to a Canadian law requiring the company to share revenue with news publishers by banning news articles from its platform altogether.) Online, the move drew outrage, including from congressional Democrats who will soon hold newfound legislative and subpoena powers. “Google is once again prioritizing profits over people,” Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut posted . “Clearly, the Tech Giant is more concerned with forcing Gemini into schools than enabling students to succeed.” Google contended that the anger was based on a misunderstanding. “Today’s announcements give schools more choice, not less ,” the company posted on X, evincing a faith in the power of boldface font to get its message across. That much is true. Google has never offered schools an AI-free version of its search engine (though there is a “Web” tab that limits results to links). What was new in Google’s announcement was that both Gemini and Search will now be turned off by default, and schools will have the option to enable one or both. For schools that enable Search, the company is touting a new “guided learning” mode in its AI features that will prompt students to work through questions one step at a time, rather than simply giving them the answer. That could help address one of the biggest objections to Google’s AI search tools in the classroom, which is that they short-circuit the learning process. (A spokesperson for the company declined to comment beyond pointing me to its public statements.) [ Read: My son’s math homework is essentially just Pokemon ] Yet Google’s response to the blowback failed to address the aspect of its announcement that had upset people in the first place. The company wasn’t taking away any options that had existed before, but it also wasn’t providing the one option schools seemed to want most: a way to let students use Google Search without also enabling the AI bells and whistles. The unspoken logic behind the company’s stance is that, in some sense, all Search is AI search. AI Overviews and AI Mode launched in 2024 and 2025, respectively, but the company has been using large language models to help rank its search results since well before the arrival of ChatGPT. Google also used AI for years to help power the precursors to AI Overviews, including “featured snippets”—those bolded excerpts from web results that Google surfaced atop its list of links. So when Google says that opting out of AI entails opting out of Search, that’s technically true. Even so, there’s something obtuse about Google’s refusal to acknowledge that consumers—and schools especially—might reasonably draw a distinction between LLMs that help power search results and LLMs that generate answers themselves. Parents and teachers mostly don’t object to Google using AI to decide which webpages to link to when students ask a question (though there is a case to be made that the company’s opaque ranking process has always deserved more scrutiny than it’s received). They object to turning Google into an instant-answer machine—and an error-prone one, at that. They object to students being conditioned to delegate their critical-thinking and source-evaluation skills to a machine. And they object to infusing the same site that indexes the world’s online information with a chatbot that can function as an ersatz friend or dispense personal advice to impressionable children. Which brings us to the business logic underlying Google’s stubborn stance. The company built its empire around a search tool that offered the shortest path between a user’s question and the information they were seeking. For years, that mostly meant refining its algorithm to downgrade spammy sites in its results. Then came ChatGPT, which promised to answer just about anything a user could ask, dispensing with the list of links altogether. OpenAI claimed this week that ChatGPT now handles about one-fifth as many search queries as Google. Chatbots are the most significant threat to Google’s core business that the search giant has ever faced. Its response has been to morph Search into an AI-answer tool in its own right. A few discontented users have dropped Google for niche alternatives such as DuckDuckGo, the privacy-focused search engine that now touts AI-free search as a selling point. Kamyl Bazbaz, a DuckDuckGo spokesperson, told me that usage of the company’s “No-AI” search option is up 30 percent since September. The company is now looking for ways to make it easier for schools that opt out of Google Search to switch their default search engine, he added. But Google seems to be betting that convenience will win out over qualms about generative AI. That bet could easily pay off, given how accustomed students already are to the tools Google has provided them with. While researching this story, I asked Google for data on how many Chromebooks are in U.S. schools. The site responded with an AI Overview confidently asserting that 93 percent of U.S. school districts plan to purchase Chromebooks. In small print, the overview cited one source for that figure: an article from a website called commandlinux.com. Skeptical, I did what fewer and fewer Google users are doing these days: I clicked on the link. The article, which appeared to be AI-written, offers no methodology or original source for any of the figures it provides. I took those extra steps because I’m a professional journalist who covers AI and its limitations for a living, and because my own schooling trained me to seek out original sources and evaluate their credibility. Had I grown up with AI search, as today’s kids do, I doubt I would have thought to question the number that Google handed me.

items.title: Hamzat seeks stronger private sector role in Lagos development
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — Lagos State Deputy Governor and All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate for the 2027 election, Dr Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, has called for stronger public-private sector collaboration, improved revenue generation and sustained infrastructure investment to drive the state’s long-term development. Hamzat made the call on Wednesday at an investment management engagement tagged, “The Exclusive Investment Parley with Dr Kadri Obafemi Hamzat”, organised by Aztran Company on Lagos Island. He said governance was more complex than running a private business because government institutions had to cater to everyone while managing competing social and economic demands. “Governance is far more complex than running a private business because the government does not have the luxury of choosing who it serves; it must serve everyone. That is why strengthening public-private sector collaboration is critical to delivering sustainable development for Lagos,” he said. Comparing Lagos State’s N4.4 trillion budget with New York City’s $109 billion budget, Hamzat said the next phase of development in Lagos required sustaining existing investments and expanding the resources available for infrastructure delivery. He said the state government had recorded achievements in socioeconomic and political development, citing the successful implementation of 11 Oracle Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) modules. According to him, the reforms improved financial accountability, eliminated ghost workers and revenue leakages, and significantly boosted the state’s internally generated revenue. Hamzat also cited the state’s ability to finance major infrastructure projects, including rail development, as evidence of its capacity to execute complex projects despite limited resources. On waste management, the deputy governor reaffirmed the government’s commitment to reforming the sector through improved funding arrangements, efficient waste collection and increased support for Private Sector Participants (PSPs). He explained that the government was reviewing the existing collection model to enable PSP operators to receive payments directly from the government rather than depending solely on collections from residents. He added that subsidies would be sustained to cushion the impact of rising operational costs on waste management operators. Earlier, the Co-Managing Partner of Aztran, Victor Aluyi, called for deeper collaboration between the private sector and the Lagos State Government, urging investors to mobilise capital to bridge the state’s infrastructure financing gap. Aluyi said government funding alone could not meet Lagos’ growing infrastructure needs, particularly in mass transportation, power, affordable housing, waste management and logistics. He put Lagos’ estimated Gross Domestic Product at $260 billion, describing it as Africa’s second-largest city economy after Cairo. He called for greater participation by private investors, institutional funds and infrastructure financing vehicles in delivering projects capable of supporting the state’s economic growth. Citing the growth of Nigeria’s non-pension asset management industry from approximately N10.1 trillion in 2024 to N16.5 trillion in 2025, Aluyi urged deliberate efforts to channel more private capital into viable infrastructure projects. He said policy consistency, regulatory clarity, transparency and effective risk-sharing mechanisms were essential to attracting investors and establishing commercially sustainable partnerships. In his remarks, Olayemi Agbe-Davies identified revenue generation and tax reform as critical to strengthening Lagos’ investment climate. He said expanding the state’s revenue base through a broader, simpler and more predictable tax system would benefit both the government and investors. Agbe-Davies expressed optimism that the engagement would give investors clearer insights into emerging infrastructure opportunities and the development priorities of Hamzat ahead of the 2027 governorship election. He urged participants to sustain their commitment to long-term investment and strategic collaboration to advance Lagos’ economic growth. items.title: Over 80 deaf students in Savelugu receive practical robotics training by Untamed Voices
items.description: More than 80 students of the Savelugu School for the Deaf in the Northern Region have received practical training in robotics and basic electronics as part of an initiative to expand access to Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education for Deaf and hard-of-hearing young people. The two-day programme, organised by youth-led non-profit Untamed Voices under its Deaf & Dynamic Initiative, introduced students to Arduino-based projects, alongside sessions on self-advocacy, breast cancer awareness and creative expression. The initiative was implemented in partnership with FemAid360 and Golden Inspire Foundation to provide practical skills and knowledge that support their education and future career opportunities. On the second day, participants took part in hands-on STEM sessions, learning how to use Arduino kits to develop basic electronic projects. The exercises introduced them to engineering, electronics and coding, giving them a chance to explore technology through practical activities. Organisers said the sessions were a new experience for the participating students and teachers, but the students showed enthusiasm and interest in the activities. Five students to receive continued STEM support To sustain the programme beyond the two-day engagement, Untamed Voices plans to establish a STEM club at the school. Five students identified for their interest and potential in the subject to receive longer-term support and mentorship. Untamed Voices Director Vincent Yovo said the initiative was designed to identify and nurture talent while creating opportunities for Deaf young people to participate in technology and innovation. “Deaf students deserve equitable access to practical STEM education and opportunities to explore technology, engineering, and innovation,” he said. He noted that access to hands-on learning and sustained technical mentorship remained limited in some educational settings. The proposed STEM club is expected to give students an opportunity to build on the skills acquired during the programme through continued learning, experimentation and technical development. Programme combines STEM, health education and personal development The first day focused on self-advocacy and personal development, encouraging students to understand their needs, express themselves and build confidence. Participants also received breast cancer awareness education and took part in screening activities facilitated through the partnership with Golden Inspire Foundation. Art activities also gave students another opportunity to communicate their ideas, experiences, and perspectives through creative expression. Untamed Voices said the programme forms part of its broader efforts to expand opportunities for Deaf and hard-of-hearing young people through digital literacy, STEM education, leadership development and practical skills training. The organisation hopes the initiative will help address gaps in access to technology and mentorship while supporting the participation of Deaf young people in education, employment, entrepreneurship and society.

items.title: Le souverain marocain ordonne au gouvernement la prise en charge du processus de retrait de la MINURSO du pays
items.description: Le souverain marocain Mohammed VI a chargé le ministère de l'Intérieur de coordonner les procédures de liquidation et de retrait de la Mission des Nations unies (MINURSO), après que le Conseil de sécurité de l'ONU ait décidé, lors de sa réunion du 30 octobre, de ne pas renouveler son mandat. Le communiqué indique que le souverain marocain a donné instruction au « Bureau de coordination avec la MINURSO », rattaché au ministère de l’Intérieur, de prendre en charge le suivi du processus de retrait de la mission et de coordonner les mesures y afférentes avec les Nations unies, afin d’en garantir le bon déroulement. Il a ajouté que le roi avait souligné, lors d’une réunion au palais royal de Rabat, la nécessité de suivre l’évolution du dossier du Sahara à différents niveaux et de poursuivre les projets de développement dans les provinces du sud, tout en insistant sur l’engagement du Maroc à respecter le cessez-le-feu, malgré la fin du mandat de la mission onusienne. Le Maroc a réaffirmé son attachement à la proposition d’autonomie, considérée, selon le communiqué, comme la seule solution politique au conflit, en rappelant la reconnaissance par des pays amis et frères de sa souveraineté sur le Sahara. La réunion a rassemblé la cheffe du gouvernement Fatima Zahra Mansouri, le conseiller du roi Fouad Ali El Himma, le ministre de l’Intérieur Abdelouafi Laftit et l’inspecteur général des Forces armées royales Mohamed Bariz.

« La sécurité du Niger est celle de l’Algérie » : Alger réaffirme son soutien sans réserve à Niamey…
items.description: À l’occasion du 72ᵉ anniversaire du déclenchement de la Révolution algérienne, l’ambassadeur d’Algérie au Niger, M. Saadi Ahmed, a réaffirmé, mardi 3 novembre 2026 à Niamey, la détermination de son pays à approfondir ses excellentes relations avec le Niger. Énergie, défense, formation, infrastructures et échanges commerciaux : le diplomate a présenté les principaux axes d’une coopération appelée à traduire les liens historiques de fraternité en réalisations concrètes. La cérémonie a réuni des membres du Conseil national pour la sauvegarde de la patrie (CNSP), du gouvernement et des institutions de la République, ainsi que des représentants du corps diplomatique et de nombreux amis de l’Algérie. Au-delà de la commémoration, cette rencontre a permis de dresser un panorama des relations bilatérales, dans un contexte où les deux pays entendent renforcer leur concertation et conjuguer leurs efforts face aux défis de sécurité et de développement au Sahel. Revenant sur le sens du 1ᵉʳ novembre 1954, M. Saadi Ahmed a rappelé que cette date avait ouvert la voie à la lutte ayant conduit à l’indépendance de l’Algérie, proclamée le 5 juillet 1962. Il a évoqué les 132 années de colonisation française et rendu hommage au sacrifice de plus d’un million et demi de martyrs. Le diplomate a également insisté sur le rayonnement africain de la Révolution algérienne, présentée comme une source d’inspiration pour les peuples engagés dans leur émancipation. Évoquant la place de l’Algérie dans l’imaginaire des luttes de libération, il a repris l’image d’une terre de référence pour les révolutionnaires, comme La Mecque pour le pèlerinage musulman ou le Vatican pour les fidèles catholiques. Ce rappel historique a servi de fil conducteur à son intervention . Pour l’ambassadeur, la solidarité avec le Niger s’inscrit dans le prolongement d’un attachement à la souveraineté, à la liberté des peuples et à la coopération africaine. M. Saadi Ahmed a surtout insisté sur le caractère indissociable des destins des deux pays. « L’Algérie est contre toute forme d’attaque, et a réaffirmé que la sécurité du Niger touche directement celle de l’Algérie », soulignant ainsi, la volonté d’Alger de soutenir Niamey dans la préservation de sa stabilité et de sa souveraineté. Le diplomate a également été salué pour sa connaissance approfondie du Niger, où il a déjà servi. Frère et ami du pays, il est présenté comme un acteur expérimenté, rompu aux réalités du terrain et aux priorités de la coopération bilatérale. Son dynamisme, souligné lors de la rencontre, est perçu comme un atout pour accélérer la mise en œuvre des engagements pris par les deux États. La volonté de consolider les relations entre Alger et Niamey repose d’abord sur l’engagement de leurs dirigeants. Le président algérien, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a notamment réaffirmé la disponibilité de son pays à répondre à toute demande officielle d’assistance de ses voisins : « Nous soutiendrons le Niger s’il nous le demande officiellement, de même que le Mali, et nous répondrons présents. » Cette position traduit une approche revendiquée de bon voisinage et de respect de la souveraineté des États. Le soutien algérien au Niger, a rappelé le diplomate, concerne plusieurs domaines, du développement à l’énergie, en passant par la coopération militaire. La visite de fraternité et de travail effectuée à Alger, les 15 et 16 février 2026, par le président nigérien, le général d’armée Abdourahamane Tiani, a constitué une étape importante de ce rapprochement. Invité par son homologue algérien, le chef de l’État était accompagné d’une délégation comprenant notamment les responsables de la Défense nationale, des Affaires étrangères, de l’Énergie, du Pétrole et des Infrastructures. Face à la menace terroriste, aux trafics illicites et aux difficultés de contrôle des frontières, la coopération de défense occupe une place croissante dans les relations algéro-nigériennes. Il faut souligner que dans le cadre de notre coopération, l’Algérie a fourni à l’armée nigérienne quatre hélicoptères, ainsi que des équipements, des munitions, des pièces de rechange et des moyens de maintenance et de soutien logistique. Il faut rappeler que sur instructions du président Abdelmadjid Tebboune, deux patrouilles de chasseurs Sukhoï Su-30, soit quatre appareils, accompagnées d’un avion de transport militaire et d’un avion ravitailleur, ont également été dépêchées dans la capitale nigérienne le 30 août 2026. Cette intervention, annoncée par le ministère algérien de la Défense nationale, visait à soutenir la sécurisation de l’espace aérien du Niger. Au-delà de ces appuis matériels, les échanges portent sur le renseignement, la surveillance des frontières communes, la lutte contre le terrorisme et la gestion des flux migratoires. La signature, le 21 octobre 2026, d’un protocole d’accord militaire a donné un cadre supplémentaire à cette coopération. Celui-ci couvre notamment la formation, l’équipement, la santé, le renforcement des capacités et la sécurisation des grands projets communs. L’objectif affiché est de passer d’une assistance ponctuelle à une collaboration durable et coordonnée. Le secteur énergétique constitue un autre axe majeur du partenariat. Les visites du ministre d’État algérien chargé des Hydrocarbures à Niamey, fin janvier, puis les 21 et 22 septembre 2026, ont notamment permis d’examiner les dossiers pétroliers et l’avancement du gazoduc transsaharien. Dans le domaine de l’électricité, l’ambassadeur a mis en avant l’extension de la centrale de solidarité de 40 MW de Gorou Banda, destinée à améliorer l’approvisionnement de Niamey et de sa périphérie. Son inauguration a accompagné la dynamique de coopération portée par les deux gouvernements, notamment lors de la visite du Premier ministre algérien, Sifi Ghrieb, au Niger. Sur le volet pétrolier, le lancement du puits d’exploration « Kafra Sud-Est 1 », le 13 août 2026 dans la région d’Agadez, figure parmi les réalisations phares. Conduit par ENAFOR, filiale de Sonatrach, en partenariat avec la Sonidep, ce forage vise, selon les estimations évoquées, à confirmer un potentiel de plus de 260 millions de barils. Le gazoduc transsaharien demeure, quant à lui, l’un des projets les plus ambitieux. Destiné à relier le Nigeria à l’Algérie en traversant le Niger, cet ouvrage d’environ 4 000 kilomètres, dont le coût est estimé à 13 milliards de dollars, doit contribuer à l’intégration énergétique régionale et à la diversification des voies d’approvisionnement en gaz. M. Saadi Ahmed a rappelé l’annonce, lors des échanges de février 2026, du lancement d’un premier tronçon passant par le Niger. Il a également évoqué la poursuite des négociations techniques et le démarrage de travaux dans la wilaya algérienne d’Adrar, tandis que les consultations de septembre ont porté sur le tracé nigérien et les modalités de réalisation. La coopération ne se limite pas aux infrastructures et aux équipements. L’Algérie a également accordé au Niger un programme de 500 bourses de formation professionnelle dans différents métiers techniques et domaines liés à la sécurité. À travers cette initiative, les deux pays entendent favoriser le transfert de compétences, renforcer les capacités des institutions nigériennes et développer des relations durables entre leurs établissements de formation. L’enjeu est aussi de permettre à la jeunesse de mieux accéder aux possibilités d’emploi liées aux projets communs. Dans le domaine numérique, l’ambassadeur a salué l’inauguration, le 6 octobre dernier, de l’interconnexion à fibre optique entre l’Algérie et le Niger. Il a également souligné les perspectives offertes par l’ouverture des ports algériens aux produits nigériens et par l’installation annoncée d’une succursale bancaire algérienne à Niamey. Ces initiatives doivent accompagner le développement des échanges et faciliter les opérations des acteurs économiques des deux pays. Pour les deux partenaires, le principal enjeu reste désormais l’exécution des engagements. La finalisation des accords techniques et contractuels, la mobilisation des financements et la clarification des garanties d’investissement figurent parmi les conditions nécessaires à l’aboutissement des projets. Le suivi devra également reposer sur des calendriers précis, des comités de pilotage bilatéraux et une évaluation régulière des retombées économiques et sociales. La Haute Commission mixte, les consultations sectorielles et un tableau de bord commun des projets sont appelés à soutenir cette coordination. Pour le Niger, cette coopération ouvre des perspectives en matière d’accès aux capacités techniques, industrielles et énergétiques, mais aussi de valorisation des ressources et de diversification des débouchés commerciaux. Pour l’Algérie, elle s’inscrit dans une démarche de coopération Sud-Sud et de consolidation des liens avec son voisinage sahélien. En clôturant son intervention, M. Saadi Ahmed a réaffirmé l’attachement de son pays aux relations historiques, humaines et culturelles qui l’unissent au Niger. Il a formulé des vœux de paix, de stabilité et de prospérité pour le peuple nigérien, tout en appelant à poursuivre l’élargissement d’un partenariat au service du développement et de l’intégration africaine. Par Tamtaminfo News L’article « La sécurité du Niger est celle de l’Algérie » : Alger réaffirme son soutien sans réserve à Niamey… est apparu en premier sur Tamtaminfo .

items.title: Un financement allemand : 15 millions d’euros pour soutenir l’emploi à travers le financement de petites et moyennes entreprises en Mauritanie
items.description: Le ministre des Affaires économiques et du Développement, Mouhamedou Ahmedou Mhaimid, a signé mardi à Nouakchott, avec la conseillère régionale de la Banque allemande de reconstruction (KfW), Sonja Haus, un accord de financement d’un montant de 15 millions d’euros, soit environ 675 millions MRU, destiné à soutenir l’emploi en Mauritanie par le biais du financement des petites et moyennes entreprises. Ce financement vise à fournir des ressources financières répondant aux besoins des petites et moyennes entreprises, afin de favoriser la création de valeur, la croissance et la création d’emplois. Le ministre a déclaré que la Mauritanie et l’Allemagne entretenaient un partenariat solide et fructueux dans plusieurs secteurs économiques et sociaux, soulignant que l’emploi constituait un domaine important de la coopération entre les deux pays et que la mobilisation des ressources représentait un défi pour les petites et moyennes entreprises. De son côté, l’ambassadeur allemand a déclaré que cet accord constituait une étape importante dans le renforcement des relations d’amitié et de coopération entre les deux pays, ajoutant qu’il reflétait leur volonté de poursuivre un partenariat fondé sur la confiance mutuelle et un dialogue ouvert, et exprimant son espoir qu’il contribue à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des jeunes Mauritaniens.

items.title: Agalga rejects cocaine probe by Parliament, says criminal investigations lie outside its powers
items.description: Majority Leader James Agalga has rejected the Minority’s push for a parliamentary probe into cocaine seizures, saying the House has no power to conduct criminal investigations. Speaking on JoyNews’ PM Express on Wednesday, he accused the Minority of pursuing an inquiry despite knowing the limits of Parliament’s authority. “Parliament has not got the power to conduct criminal investigations.” He said the Minority’s demand amounted to an attempt to play to the gallery while investigative agencies were already handling the cases. “The minority is aware that Parliament is not clothed with the power to carry out criminal investigations.” Mr Agalga said arrests and court proceedings were already underway. Some suspects had been arraigned, others had been granted bail, and trials were ongoing in some cases. He questioned what Parliament would investigate under those circumstances. His comments follow the Minority’s petition for Parliament to be recalled from recess over major narcotics seizures linked to Ghana. The caucus sought scrutiny of port security, cargo inspections and the work of agencies responsible for preventing drug trafficking. Speaker Alban Bagbin subsequently recalled the House for an emergency sitting on September 29. He ruled the proposed inquiry inadmissible in its current form. The Speaker said its scope substantially overlapped with matters before the courts. He warned that proceeding could prejudice parties involved in pending judicial proceedings. The ruling prevented the proposed inquiry from going ahead as presented. Mr Agalga also invoked the sub judice principle, arguing that Parliament’s rules restricted its involvement in matters already before the judiciary. “Parliament’s own standing orders will not allow us to stray into matters that have engaged the attention of the judiciary. The minority knows this.”
