items.title: Areeba Guinée : Mamy Diaby prend les commandes et annonce une restructuration profonde
items.description: Areeba Guinée SA amorce un nouveau virage. Installé ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 au poste de directeur général, Mamy Diaby annonce une restructuration profonde de l’entreprise, confrontée à de sérieuses difficultés financières, techniques et opérationnelles. Rationalisation des coûts, modernisation du réseau, relance commerciale et transformation du modèle économique figurent parmi les cinq axes de son plan de redressement. Mohamed Diallo a également été installé comme directeur général adjoint. La cérémonie de passation de service entre le directeur général par intérim sortant, Djemori Kouyaté, et son successeur s’est déroulée au siège de l’entreprise, à Coléah, en présence des travailleurs, des représentants syndicaux et des autorités de tutelle. Prenant la parole, Mamy Diaby a d’abord exprimé sa reconnaissance au président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, pour la confiance placée en lui à travers cette nomination. « À cette occasion, permettez-moi de remercier vivement Son Excellence Monsieur le Président Mamadi Doumbouya pour la confiance placée à ma modeste personne en me nommant à ce poste stratégique dont les défis sont légion et les responsabilités on ne peut plus importantes… J’ai d’ailleurs conscience que cette confiance est un appel au travail sans faille, à l’engagement patriotique permanent et je ferai tout pour la mériter avec la grâce de Dieu et j’espère le soutien constant de mes équipes », a-t-il déclaré. Il a également rendu hommage à son prédécesseur pour les efforts consentis durant les onze mois passés à la tête de l’entreprise par intérim. « À mon cher frère, monsieur Kouyaté qui m’a précédé à ce poste, je salue votre dévouement et votre lutte franche à préserver et à maintenir l’intégrité du réseau. Je salue ici votre résilience et je vous dis grand merci », a-t-il souligné. Un diagnostic préoccupant et cinq axes de restructuration Le nouveau directeur général n’a pas caché l’ampleur des difficultés auxquelles Areeba Guinée est confrontée. Il a notamment évoqué le manque d’investissements technologiques, la baisse des marges sur les services traditionnels, les tensions de trésorerie, la concurrence accrue ainsi que les perturbations qui affectent parfois la qualité des services. « Nous faisons face à un manque d’investissement technologique, à la baisse des marges sur les services classiques ou traditionnels comme la voix, à des problèmes de trésorerie, à une concurrence accrue et à des crises opérationnelles qui ont parfois perturbé la qualité de nos services et l’expérience de nos clients. Malgré les efforts constants consentis par chacun d’entre vous, les derniers résultats financiers montrent que notre entreprise est fragile, que le modèle actuel ne fonctionne plus », a-t-il reconnu. Pour lui, de simples ajustements ne permettront pas de sortir l’entreprise de cette situation. Il entend donc engager immédiatement un plan de restructuration profonde et globale reposant sur cinq piliers. Le premier consiste à rationaliser les coûts opérationnels afin de retrouver rapidement des marges de manœuvre financières et d’éviter une faillite immédiate ainsi qu’une éventuelle fermeture du réseau. Le deuxième axe porte sur la stabilisation des opérations et des infrastructures techniques. Le troisième prévoit de recentrer les investissements sur les activités à forte valeur ajoutée, notamment le déploiement des infrastructures, les nouvelles technologies et l’amélioration de l’expérience client. Le quatrième pilier vise à renforcer la réponse commerciale et la fidélisation des abonnés, tandis que le cinquième concerne la transformation durable de l’entreprise, à travers la redéfinition de son modèle économique. Cette restructuration pourrait toutefois entraîner des changements importants dans l’organisation interne et les méthodes de travail. « Cette transformation exigera des efforts partagés et entraînera des changements importants dans nos méthodes de travail et dans notre organisation humaine. Au nom de toute la direction, je m’engage à ce que ce processus se déroule avec une transparence totale, le respect de chacun et un dialogue social constructif et permanent avec vos représentants. La restructuration n’est pas un objectif en soi, cela est un passage obligatoire pour assurer notre survie puis notre relance », a-t-il prévenu. Malgré ce tableau préoccupant, Mamy Diaby estime que l’entreprise dispose encore d’atouts importants pour réussir son redressement, notamment son réseau, sa clientèle et les compétences de ses travailleurs. « Nous disposons d’actifs précieux, d’un réseau étendu, d’une base clientèle et surtout du capital de compétences exceptionnelles au sein de l’entreprise », a-t-il rappelé. Djemori Kouyaté revient sur onze mois de gestion sous pression Avant de passer le relais, le directeur général par intérim sortant, Djemori Kouyaté, est revenu sur les onze mois particulièrement éprouvants passés à la tête de l’entreprise, après le départ définitif du groupe MTN. Il a évoqué une période marquée par de nombreuses difficultés techniques, financières et énergétiques, mais aussi par les efforts déployés pour maintenir les activités et préserver les emplois. « Voici arrivé à terme ma mission après 11 mois d’exercice à temps plein et de combat acharné pour conduire les activités de la société à la suite du départ définitif du groupe MTN. 11 mois passés dans une atmosphère d’incertitude mais très conviviale, pacifique avec les collaborateurs combattants armés de volonté et de courage, espérant l’accompagnement du gouvernement qui, par la volonté politique du chef de l’État, président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, a décidé de faire de la société Areeba un patrimoine national avec l’idée de redynamiser le secteur du numérique en Guinée », a-t-il rappelé. Parmi les principaux défis rencontrés, il a cité le vieillissement des équipements, les difficultés d’accès à l’énergie et la rude concurrence sur le marché des télécommunications. « 11 mois d’intense activité, parsemée d’embûches certes, mais dont l’objectif a été de rassurer et de garantir les emplois directs et indirects. 11 mois de bricolage d’équipements complètement vétustes, de difficultés d’accès à l’énergie, de lutte farouche de maintien sur le marché face à la rude concurrence », a-t-il résumé. Sur le plan financier, Djemori Kouyaté a également fait état des tensions de trésorerie, liées notamment à la baisse progressive des revenus et à l’absence d’investissements du groupe MTN au cours des dix dernières années. Il a néanmoins salué l’accompagnement de l’État, qui aurait permis de préserver les acquis sociaux des travailleurs. « C’était aussi et surtout 11 mois de sourire des employés et de leur famille car au cours desquels, ils ont perçu régulièrement et à temps l’ensemble des droits et avantages liés à leur fonction respective, malgré les difficultés financières auxquelles la société a été confrontée depuis quelques années », a-t-il souligné. Sur le volet technique, il a annoncé que des travaux d’installation de batteries étaient en cours sur une centaine de sites à Conakry et à l’intérieur du pays, dans le but de réduire l’instabilité énergétique et la dépendance au carburant. Il a toutefois prévenu que ces interventions ne représentent qu’une partie des besoins de modernisation du réseau. « La modernisation des sites concernés n’est que très, très partielle et ne constitue qu’une infime partie des besoins eu égard à la taille du chantier qui requiert une modernisation complète du réseau. L’espoir de trouver un financement structurant pour ce joyau de la téléphonie tant attendu par nos populations et ayant révolutionné ce secteur en Guinée en 2006, à l’effet de le voir reprendre sa place d’antan », a-t-il déclaré. Il a enfin réaffirmé sa disponibilité à accompagner la nouvelle direction dans l’accomplissement de sa mission. « Je vous rassure de ma disponibilité à vous soutenir, à vous accompagner dans votre noble mission que prie Allah le Tout-Puissant de couronner de succès », a-t-il affirmé. Le syndicat appelle à accompagner la nouvelle direction Au nom des travailleurs, le secrétaire général du bureau syndical d’Areeba, Jérôme Cécé Haba, a salué le travail accompli par Djemori Kouyaté et souhaité la bienvenue aux nouveaux responsables. « Djemory Kouyaté est de nous et il reste de nous. Nous avons toujours évolué même dans nos activités syndicales avec lui, bien entendu avant qu’il ne soit directeur général par intérim », a-t-il déclaré. S’adressant aux travailleurs, il les a invités à accompagner la nouvelle équipe dirigeante dans ses efforts de redressement, tout en rappelant l’importance du respect du Code du travail et des obligations contractuelles. « Nous restons, comme je le disais hier à notre assemblée générale, sous la gouverne du Code du travail et de nos contrats. Nous sommes tenus au respect : celui qui réclame droit doit d’abord avoir fait son devoir », a-t-il rappelé. Le responsable syndical a également insisté sur la nécessité d’une mobilisation collective pour permettre à l’entreprise de retrouver sa place sur le marché. « Je dis que je nous encourage à faire davantage, à soutenir la direction générale qui nous est donnée pour un travail performant, pour un travail producteur, pour que la société Areeba retrouve sa place d’antan et que ce soit pour nous un orgueil national de nous bomber la poitrine. Notre situation d’employés reste marquée par beaucoup d’inquiétudes. Avec la nouvelle direction, nous espérons que cela va beaucoup plus avancer au-delà de la situation de l’entreprise qui relève beaucoup plus du management », a-t-il soutenu. Il a cependant soulevé une préoccupation persistante concernant les conditions salariales des employés. « Il y a pratiquement une décennie que, s’il y a avantage ou augmentation substantielle, les travailleurs d’Areeba ne connaissent pas », a-t-il déploré. L’État mise sur le redressement d’un opérateur national Représentant le ministère de la Communication, de l’Économie numérique et de l’Innovation, le secrétaire général, Souleymane Thiâ’nguel Bah, a insisté sur la nécessité de consolider l’équipe autour du nouveau directeur général. Pour lui, la réussite de cette mission dépendra largement de l’engagement collectif des travailleurs. « Mamy vient dans un endroit où vous êtes déjà une équipe, il faut que vous trouviez un petit trou, un espace dans lequel il peut s’insérer. Faites cela, afin qu’il puisse compter sur vous, qu’il puisse être là lorsque vous avez besoin d’une aide ou d’un appui », a-t-il lancé. Le représentant du département a surtout mis en avant l’enjeu stratégique que représente le redressement d’Areeba pour la souveraineté numérique de la Guinée et l’équilibre du marché des télécommunications. « Il y a aujourd’hui dans notre pays, comme vous le savez, un besoin crucial d’un opérateur national. Nous avons un opérateur privé qui a l’ensemble du marché quasiment de notre téléphonie mobile et aujourd’hui nos populations n’arrêtent pas de s’en plaindre », a-t-il déclaré. Souleymane Thiâ’nguel Bah a également rappelé que le redressement de l’entreprise s’inscrit dans une dynamique portée par les autorités, sous l’impulsion du président de la République et du gouvernement. Il a notamment évoqué le travail engagé par le ministre Mourana Soumah, avec l’appui du Premier ministre et la vision du chef de l’État, pour permettre à Areeba de retrouver sa place dans le secteur. « Il est de la responsabilité de chacune de nos sociétés de téléphonie mobile et en particulier celle-là, puisqu’on sait ce qu’elle était et ce qu’elle est capable de faire, que cette société-là se relève et qu’elle fasse face à la société privée. Le travail qui a été entamé par monsieur le ministre Mourana Soumah, il faut que ce travail-là continue. C’est une dimension, c’est un objectif qu’il s’est fixé avec l’appui de monsieur le Premier ministre et la vision de monsieur le président de la République, de faire en sorte que cette société se relève », a-t-il indiqué. Il a enfin insisté sur la nécessité de disposer de femmes et d’hommes capables de porter cette ambition nationale. « Ces opérateurs nationaux ne peuvent se faire que lorsqu’il y a des femmes et des hommes derrière capables de les porter », a-t-il conclu. Avec cette nouvelle équipe dirigeante et l’annonce d’un vaste plan de restructuration, Areeba Guinée aborde une étape déterminante de son histoire. Reste désormais à traduire les engagements annoncés en actions concrètes, pour redresser l’entreprise, moderniser son réseau et lui permettre de retrouver une place importante dans le paysage des télécommunications guinéennes. Mayi Cissé L’article Areeba Guinée : Mamy Diaby prend les commandes et annonce une restructuration profonde est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : les jeunes veulent peser davantage dans la gouvernance locale.
items.description: Réunis samedi 31 octobre à Dakar, dans le cadre du programme « Parlons JOJ », des jeunes, des élus locaux et des acteurs institutionnels ont échangé sur leur participation à la gouvernance locale. Plusieurs propositions ont été formulées pour passer d'une simple consultation à une véritable co-décision. Être consultés ne suffit plus. Les jeunes veulent désormais prendre part aux décisions qui engagent l'avenir de leurs communes. C'est l'une des principales revendications exprimées lors du deuxième dialogue citoyen du programme « Parlons JOJ », organisé samedi 31 octobre par Polaris Asso, avec le soutien de l'Ambassade de Suisse au Sénégal, dans son espace jeunesse à Dakar. « Parlons JOJ » est un programme de dialogues citoyens porté par Polaris Asso, en partenariat avec l'Ambassade de Suisse au Sénégal, dans le cadre des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse Dakar 2026. Il vise à promouvoir les valeurs démocratiques, la participation citoyenne et l'engagement de la jeunesse à travers quatre dialogues réunissant des jeunes et des décideurs autour de propositions concrètes. Son ambition est de contribuer à un héritage durable des JOJ, fondé sur une jeunesse informée, engagée et pleinement associée aux décisions qui concernent son avenir. La rencontre a réuni une quarantaine de jeunes, des élus locaux, des responsables institutionnels et des représentants de partenaires internationaux autour de la place de la jeunesse dans la gouvernance locale. À l'issue des échanges, plusieurs recommandations ont été formulées pour renforcer leur implication dans la gestion des affaires publiques. Trois jeunes leaders ont notamment porté le plaidoyer autour de questions majeures : l'instauration de mécanismes permanents de concertation et de co-décision, la redynamisation des conseils de quartier et la reconnaissance du sport et des associations sportives et culturelles comme leviers de participation citoyenne et de développement local. Rapporteure nationale du Conseil consultatif des jeunes du Sénégal (CCJS), Fatou Touré a plaidé pour la mise en place, dans chaque commune, d'un cadre permanent de concertation entre les jeunes et les conseils municipaux. Elle a également proposé la création d'une ligne budgétaire spécifiquement dédiée aux initiatives de la jeunesse, afin de leur donner les moyens de concrétiser leurs projets. De son côté, Babacar Gérard Mbaye, agent municipal à Cambérène, a insisté sur la nécessité de redynamiser les conseils de quartier. Il préconise un dispositif mensuel permettant aux jeunes de consacrer une première semaine à la réflexion collective et les trois suivantes à la mise en œuvre des initiatives retenues. Le recours aux outils numériques figure également parmi ses propositions pour faciliter la participation citoyenne. Pour Pape Ousmane Badiane, conseiller municipal à Thiaroye-sur-Mer et acteur associatif, les associations sportives et culturelles (ASC) doivent être considérées comme de véritables partenaires des collectivités territoriales. Il a ainsi suggéré la création de cadres permanents de collaboration, la formalisation d'engagements citoyens annuels et la mise en place de conventions de performance sportive, culturelle et citoyenne, avec des financements municipaux liés à des objectifs précis. Vers une gouvernance intergénérationnelle Les élus présents ont également apporté leur contribution aux échanges. La mairesse de Golf Sud, Khadija Mahécore Diouf, a invité les jeunes à investir davantage les espaces de décision et à passer de la critique à la proposition, puis à l'action. Elle a défendu une approche du développement local qui associe les habitants, notamment les jeunes, à la conception et à la mise en œuvre des projets communaux. Le maire de Khombole, Magueye Boye, a pour sa part plaidé pour une gouvernance intergénérationnelle, dans laquelle les jeunes sont associés à toutes les étapes du développement communal. Il a notamment appelé à mieux prendre en compte leurs aspirations dans l'aménagement des quartiers et la conduite des politiques locales. Présente à la rencontre, Patricia Danzi, directrice générale de la Direction du développement et de la coopération (DDC) de la Suisse, a salué les propositions formulées. Elle a notamment identifié plusieurs pistes d'action, dont le renforcement des consultations publiques, l'autonomie financière des associations de jeunesse et une meilleure représentation des conseils consultatifs de jeunes dans les instances de décision. Les travaux de groupe ont également permis d'élargir les recommandations à d'autres domaines. Les participants ont notamment évoqué l'éducation citoyenne dès le plus jeune âge, le mentorat, la création de plateformes numériques d'échanges et la transformation des conseils de quartier en véritables structures d'action locale. La formation des jeunes, l'implication des femmes dans les activités sportives et culturelles ainsi que l'intégration de l'entrepreneuriat dans les initiatives des ASC ont également été mises en avant. Pour Ousseynou Gueye, directeur exécutif de Polaris Asso, l'enjeu est de rompre avec une pratique qui consiste à solliciter régulièrement les jeunes sans leur accorder une place suffisante dans les processus décisionnels. « On parle beaucoup des jeunes, mais on parle encore trop peu avec les jeunes », a-t-il souligné à l'ouverture des travaux. Il a annoncé que les recommandations issues des dialogues « Parlons JOJ » seront transmises aux plus hautes autorités du pays et feront l'objet d'un suivi. L'ambition est de faire des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026 un levier durable de renforcement de la démocratie locale et de participation citoyenne. Ce deuxième dialogue s'inscrit dans un cycle de quatre rencontres. Après un premier rendez-vous consacré aux industries culturelles et créatives, le programme prévoit un échange sur l'entrepreneuriat des jeunes, avant une rencontre de clôture destinée à remettre aux autorités nationales les recommandations prioritaires issues des différentes concertations. A.N

items.title: Beyond the bungalow gates: Why comprehensive sex education and sex negotiation skills are our children’s real protective armor
items.description: Overview The horrifying revelations emerging from Obuasi Senior High Technical School, where up to 19 female students have reportedly come forward detailing alleged sexual exploitation and abuse by members of the school’s leadership. Such a report should send chills down the spine of every parent, educator, and policymaker in Ghana. For far too long, our cultural reflex has been one of uncomfortable silence. We treat conversations about adolescent sexuality as a taboo subject. We whisper about puberty behind closed doors while continuing to believe that our teenagers live in a vacuum of innocence. The tragedy at Obuasi SHTS demonstrates that our silence is not protecting our children; it is leaving them defenseless in the face of predatory power dynamics. As a population health researcher and health education specialist with a keen interest in sexual and reproductive health, particularly adolescent sexual and reproductive health (ASRH), I view the Obuasi SHTS scandal not only as a failure of institutional safeguarding. While the reported delays and systemic blind spots are a national shame, they also represent a catastrophic breakdown in how we prepare young people to understand their bodies, their rights, and their voices. I want us all to take note, reflect and act on these points; The myth of silence as protection In many Ghanaian homes and institutions, including schools, apprenticeship settings, churches, and mosques, sex education is often reduced to a frantic, last-minute warning to “focus on your books” or “acquire a skill” and avoid pregnancy. Discussions about sexually transmitted infections (STIs), healthy relationships, consent, and bodily autonomy are frequently relegated to the background. We operate under the dangerous fallacy that if we do not talk about sex, our children will not think about it, discuss it, or encounter it. We must stop deceiving ourselves. The reality is starkly different. Every day, young people navigate biological changes, digital spaces, peer pressure, and complex social relationships. When we deny and starve Ghana adolescents age-appropriate, life-relevant, and scientifically grounded Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE), we effectively hand them over to guesswork, misinformation, peer myths, and, worst of all, manipulative adults who exploit their ignorance. I firmly believe that comprehensive sexuality education is not, as critics often claim, an invitation to promiscuity. It is a life-saving tool. Ghana urgently needs culturally responsive and context-specific CSE delivered through a holistic lens. Comprehensive sexuality education teaches young people about anatomy, consent, bodily autonomy, healthy relationships, and, most importantly, how to recognize the red flags of emotional manipulation and physical coercion. When a young Ghanaian understands what healthy boundaries look like, they are better equipped to identify inappropriate or predatory behaviour long before it escalates behind a locked bungalow door. The Power and Gap of Sex Negotiation Skills A critical missing pillar in our national discourse is sex negotiation skills. In many Ghanaian settings, this concept is rarely discussed. Yet, sex negotiation is simply the capacity of a young person to assert “ No !,” recognize the illegitimacy of inappropriate demands made by a relative, friend, teacher, religious leader, or any other authority figure, and exercise personal autonomy without fear of punishment, retaliation, or academic sabotage. In hierarchical environments such as boarding schools, the power imbalance between a student and a headmaster, headmistress, teacher, or housemaster can be immense. An adolescent summoned to an administrator’s residence faces far more than social discomfort. They may confront a frightening web of authority, fear of poor grades, threats to future opportunities, and societal pressure to remain silent. It means teaching our children that: Consent is not passive compliance. Silence, fear, intimidation, or the absence of resistance does not constitute consent. Authority does not equal ownership. No grade, favour, errand, recommendation, or opportunity is worth a student’s dignity, safety, or well-being. Support systems must be functional. Unsafe demands can only be challenged when adolescents know that immediate, confidential, and non-judgmental reporting channels exist. Teaching sexual negotiation and assertiveness skills means explicitly validating a young person’s right to reject unwanted advances, regardless of who is making them. Navigating the cultural nuances: Home, Faith and School To address these challenges, we must confront some of the cultural realities that shape Ghanaian society. Our deep-seated traditions of overly respecting elders, preserving family reputation, and maintaining religious conservatism often contribute to silence survivors of sexual abuse. Assertiveness must never be mistaken for disrespect. This is where parents, religious institutions, and school guidance and counselling units must evolve from gatekeepers of silence into proactive protectors. The role of parents: Parents can no longer afford to outsource the moral and sexual education of their children entirely to schools. The home must become a psychological sanctuary where children feel safe discussing bodily changes, relationships, concerns, and uncomfortable encounters. If a child believes that raising concerns about an adult’s behaviour will result in scolding, punishment, victim-blaming, or accusations of being “provocative,” they are far more likely to choose and remain silent. Parents must intentionally build open channels of communication so that children can speak honestly without fear of judgment or punishment. The religious paradox: Our country is a deeply religious country, and faith-based messaging holds immense sway over adolescents. Discussions in some religious spaces focus heavily on purity and piety while paying insufficient attention to the reality of sexual abuse and predatory behaviour. Religious leaders must move beyond messages that focus exclusively on abstinence and explicitly condemn abuse perpetrated by individuals in positions of power, including those within religious institutions themselves. Faith should strengthen a child’s dignity and sense of personal worth. It should never be used to guilt-trip children into silence or unquestioning submission when they experience abuse. As the Bible reminds us in 2 Timothy 1:7: “For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind.” In many secondary schools, guidance and counselling structures exist but are intertwined with chaplaincies and religious frameworks. While faith can offer important moral grounding, it must never weaponize guilt, emphasize “purity” over safety, or attempt to pray away systemic abuse. Predatory behaviour cannot be solved through spiritual platitudes alone. The school counseling unit as a safe haven: Guidance and counselling units exist in many schools, yet they are often understaffed, underfunded, or perceived primarily as disciplinary offices rather than support services. These units should operate as trusted and independent safe spaces where students can confidently report concerns involving any authority figure without fear of intimidation, retaliation, or pressure to remain silent. Students must understand that counselling services exist for their protection and that reports will be handled professionally, confidentially, and compassionately. For counselling units to be effective, they must remain insulated from school administrative politics and prioritise student welfare above institutional image. Rebuilding the system: Where do we go from here? The fallout from the Obuasi SHTS scandal, including interdictions, police investigations, and widespread public outrage, represents a critical national turning point. Holding perpetrators accountable and investigating any individuals or structures that enabled abuse is both necessary and urgent. Nevertheless, prosecution is reactive. Prevention requires structural reform. Institutionalized ASRH specialist and tailored CSE: The Ghana Education Service, Ministry of Education, and National Council for Curriculum and Assessment must move beyond outdated discomfort surrounding sexuality education and permanently integrate rights-based CSE into second-cycle institutions. Qualified ASRH specialists should play a central role in training students as well as academic and non-academic staff. Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health specialists represent a largely overlooked resource within our educational system. Unlike many traditional teachers who may feel culturally constrained or uncomfortable discussing sexual and reproductive health topics, ASRH specialists are trained to deliver objective, evidence-based, culturally sensitive, and rights-based information. They help dismantle stigma and equip young people with the language and confidence needed to identify, describe, and report boundary violations. Integrating ASRH specialists into school health programmes and collaborating with School Health Education Programme (SHEP) coordinators and school counsellors would help ensure that sex education and sex negotiation-skills training are delivered professionally, effectively, and consistently. Established ironclad and safe reporting hotlines: Students cannot be expected to report abuse through chains of command that may protect abusers. Ghana needs independent, confidential national reporting mechanisms, including digital platforms and toll-free hotlines, managed outside local school politics and linked to appropriate counselling and child protection services. End the culture of victim blaming and media exposure: As authorities such as the Minister of Gender, rightly emphasized, careless media reporting that reveals or hints at survivors’ identities inflicts further harm and discourages others from speaking out. Protecting survivors must remain our highest priority and supreme law. Conclusion No child is sent to school to barter their body for an education. The students at Obuasi SHTS were failed by adults and institutions entrusted with their protection. We must honour their courage by dismantling the walls of silence, replacing taboo with truth, and equipping every adolescent girl and boy with the language, knowledge, confidence, and support they need to say “ No ” and be respected, protected, and heard. Only then can we build schools that are not merely places of learning, but places of safety, dignity, and hope. By:

items.title: Colleague actors ignored my call to support drug advocacy – Timothy Bentum
items.description: Media personality and Lead Pastor of Grace Avenue Ministry, Timothy Bentum, has expressed disappointment over the lack of support he received from some of his colleagues in the Ghanaian movie industry when he sought their involvement in a drug abuse advocacy campaign. According to him, he had approached fellow actors, including actress Gloria Sarfo, with the intention of mobilising industry players to support an initiative aimed at raising awareness about drug abuse and its effects on young people. However, the initiative did not receive the expected response from members of the industry, leaving him disappointed. He made these revelations during an interview on Joy Prime’s Changes show, where he discussed his experiences with drug advocacy and the need for greater public support in tackling substance abuse. “I spoke to Gloria Osei Sarfo, in fact, Gloria reached out to me and said Timothy, make we do a session with our people and I even told her I’ll pay for it so we should just get them together. Nobody minded us. Nobody reached out to me,” he told the host Nikki Samonas. On the contrary, Timothy Bentum revealed that some of his colleagues reach out to him for prayer support but fail to reciprocate when he seeks their involvement in drug abuse advocacy. He expressed disappointment over what he described as a lack of support from industry players, despite the influence and reach they command as entertainers. According to him, many of his colleagues appear to be caught up in the pursuit of fame and popularity, often neglecting the importance of personal well-being and using their influence to support meaningful causes. He believes entertainers have a responsibility to look beyond their celebrity status and actively contribute to initiatives that promote healthy living and address social challenges such as drug abuse. “People are just enjoying the fame, where they are and what they’re doing. People don’t get time for self-examination and making sure that they do the right things. They think it’s some way. Nobody has time to say let’s sit down and talk sense into our heads and try to become a better group of people in the industry.” However, he acknowledged that some of his colleagues are individually seeking God, a development he commended and encouraged them to continue. He nonetheless believes that everyone will face a day of adversity at some point in life, expressing the view that such experiences may eventually compel some of them to abandon their deviant behaviours. Timothy Bentum further disclosed that he is willing to sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA), also known as a confidentiality agreement, to protect the identities of industry players who are willing to support the advocacy but remain sceptical about coming on board publicly. “It’s not a problem at all. I’m a pastor and that patient-doctor confidentiality is there. So there’s no problem at all,” he said. He believes celebrities and other public figures have an important role to play in addressing social challenges, particularly drug abuse, which continues to affect individuals, families and communities. His comments underscore the need for greater collaboration among entertainment industry players in using their platforms and influence to champion social causes. He further stressed the importance of involving influential personalities in educating young people about the dangers of drug abuse and encouraging positive behavioural change.

items.title: Bagbin is pursuing parliamentary bullying – says Afenyo-Markin
items.description: Minority Leader Osahen Alexander Afenyo-Markin has accused Speaker of Parliament Alban Bagbin of presiding over what he describes as parliamentary bullying, following the removal of Damongo MP and Ranking Member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, from the parliamentary chamber on Tuesday. Reading a statement on behalf of the Minority Caucus on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, Afenyo-Markin condemned the Speaker’s decision to maintain the directive for Abu Jinapor to leave the Chamber, despite the MP having withdrawn allegations he made concerning the alleged sale of Ghanaian diplomatic passports. Jinapor had raised concerns that diplomatic passports were being sold for amounts ranging from US$10,000 to US$50,000, prompting the Speaker to direct him to withdraw the allegations pending evidence. According to the Minority, Jinapor sought clarification on the specific allegation before expressly withdrawing his comments twice. However, the directive for him to leave the Chamber was upheld. The Minority described the action as “disproportionate, humiliating and, in its effect, an act of parliamentary bullying.” “An express withdrawal in compliance with the Speaker’s directive deserves acknowledgement, not punishment,” Afenyo-Markin said. The development triggered a walkout by Minority MPs, who said their action was in solidarity with Mr. Jinapor and in protest against what they considered an unjust treatment of their colleague. Beyond the parliamentary confrontation, the Minority insists that the allegations surrounding the issuance of diplomatic and service passports warrant a full investigation. It claims to possess supporting material raising concerns about alleged false representations and impersonation in the procurement of such passports, with indications of possible illicit transactions. The caucus has called for the material to be examined through appropriate parliamentary procedures and demanded that Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa appear before Parliament to respond to the allegations. Afenyo-Markin also accused the governing Majority of using its numerical strength to frustrate parliamentary scrutiny and undermine the rights of the Minority. He warned that parliamentary majorities must not become instruments of intimidation, arguing that electoral victories do not give governments the licence to suppress dissent or evade accountability. “The Majority may possess the votes, but the Minority must retain an effective voice and a keen eye for scrutiny,” he stated. The Minority Leader further urged Speaker Bagbin to demonstrate greater impartiality in managing parliamentary disagreements and to distinguish between legitimate dissent and disrespect. The caucus has also raised broader concerns about what it describes as a pattern of intimidation, harassment and politically motivated actions against members of the opposition, including arrests, detention and onerous bail conditions. Reaffirming the Minority’s commitment to its constitutional responsibilities, Afenyo-Markin said the caucus would not be intimidated into abandoning its oversight role. “Hon. Samuel Abu Jinapor shall not be silenced. The Minority Caucus shall not be silenced,” he declared. The Minority also pledged to continue demanding accountability from government officials and defend the constitutional rights of Parliament and the public at large.

items.title: Seeing red in Iran
items.description: IN the run-up to yesterday’s US mid-term elections , it became obvious that, almost four decades after the Cold War ended, the ‘spectre of communism’ Marx and Engels identified in the 19th century still haunts Western consciousness. Islamophobia might have been the most prominent weapon, but it was accompanied by diatribes against Marxists and communists, invariably directed against people who are neither. For good measure, some of them are simultaneously derided as Islamist jihadists. The American establishment’s obsession with the communist threat, real or imagined, dates back to the early 20th century, and has served as a guiding principle of its foreign (and domestic) policy since the Truman era. One of the CIA’s first interventions, against Iranian democracy in the early 1950s, was justified as a blow against communist influence, even though the popular nationalist Mohammad Mossadegh was barely left of centre. Furthermore, the communist party Tudeh had initially misidentified him as a mole for US interests, recognising only belatedly that his oil nationalisation was in Iran’s interest. The party was decimated in the wake of the CIA-guided coup that re-established the Shah’s reign, under the aegis of Savak, MI6, and Mossad. The survivors fled abroad, mostly ending up in East Germany, although many underground operatives remained in situ, and retained some influence in the military arm of the state. Thus, when Tudeh resurfaced in the lead-up to the 1979 revolution, it wasn’t starting from scratch. It participated in the mass surge against the tyrannical Shah, but, unlike the militant Mujahideen-i-Khalq and others on the left, acknowledged the Khomeini phenomenon as a legitimate expression of the popular will. That helps to explain why Tudeh briefly became the main opposition in a milieu dominated by the Islamic Republican Party. It’s unlikely this arrangement would anyhow have lasted long, but things came to a head in 1982-83. The US today faces its own Great Game fallout. The saga is laid out in entertaining detail in espionage specialist author Ben Macin­t­yre’s recently published Redwood — a fascinating, albeit somewhat breathless, account of the defection in Tehran of a senior KGB officer, Vladimir Kuzichkin, the Soviet point man for contacts with Tudeh and a network of spies. In Macintyre’s reading, Kuzichkin was disillusioned with his corrupt colleagues, as well as with the Soviet polity, but above all, it was his impotence that drove him to risk approaching MI6, expecting Western medicine to offer a cure. (Viagra was more than a decade away, but MI6 was able to organise a discreet circumcision.) More significantly, Kuzichkin passed on to MI6’s Ian McCredie his list of Iranian contacts and details of communications with Moscow. MI6 shared them with the CIA, which was unable to operate in Iran at the time, and the latter insisted on sharing them with Iran’s intelligence agencies. Iran had only recently released the hostages taken at the US embassy, but while the American cold warriors might not have been fans of the clergy, in their blinkered worldview the communist threat was paramount. MI6 was happy, as always, to play second fiddle. The suspicion was that Moscow’s arms and gold were preparing Tudeh for a coup that could pave the way for a Soviet invasion, as in Afghanistan, and further tilt the Cold War imbalance towards communism. By 1982, it should have been obvious to Moscow that the Afghan occupation was going awry — thanks largely to the CIA’s covert war via Pakistan. Macintyre does not mention Zbigniew Brzezinski’s role, through the CIA and regional assets, in luring the Red Army into its biggest folly. But, giv­en the state of aff­airs in the nei­­ghbourhood, it’s unl­ikely Moscow wou­ld seriously have contemplated a sim­ilar misadventure in Iran. Non­etheless, it was decided to impart Redwood’s information to the Iranian authorities, and the chosen venue was Islamabad, courtesy of the then ISI chief Gen Abdul Rehman Akhtar. Even though senior elements of the Iranian leadership — including Ayatollah Khomeini, parliamentary speaker Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, and prime minister Mir-Hossein Mousavi — had their doubts about the imminence of a communist coup attempt and advised restraint, the president Ali Khamenei and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps chief Mohsen Rezaei favoured haste, leading to thousands of arrests and mass executions, alongside torture and televised ‘confessions’. As in Afghanistan earlier this century, the US is today confronted, in part, with the consequences of its own Great Game machinations. But ask any surviving cold warrior, and most likely they’ll still contend it was a price worth paying for keeping the world safe from communism. Many of us, meanwhile, awaiting this week’s election results, look forward to the impending demise of the American empire. mahir.dawn@gmail.com Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

items.title: Jaxaay accueille le Quartier général des Joj territorialisées
items.description: Les Joj « Dakar 2026 » constituent un levier de développement communautaire et de démocratisation de l’accès au sport. Dans le cadre du partenariat conclu en mai 2026 entre l’Agence de développement municipal (Adm) et le Comité d’organisation des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (Cojoj), des infrastructures de proximité sont réalisées dans les départements de Pikine, Guédiawaye, Keur Massar et Rufisque pour pérenniser l’héritage olympique. Les terrains multifonctionnels de Dalifort (Pikine) et de Keur Massar Nord ont été inaugurés , dans le cadre d’un programme de plus de 2,2 milliards de FCfa, soutenu par la Banque mondiale et le Fonds nordique de développement (Ndf). Il comprend six terrains de football en gazon synthétique, deux terrains multifonctionnels, des parcours sportifs et des espaces paysagers. Leur gestion repose sur un Comité technique de suivi et des Cellules olympiques communales réunissant acteurs locaux, associations sportives et services de l’éducation. En parallèle, des activités sportives, culturelles et écocitoyennes ont été lancées dans 13 communes. Plus de 650 athlètes s’affrontent dans dix disciplines, dont le football, le basketball, la lutte traditionnelle, le cyclisme, les arts martiaux et la randonnée. Cette mobilisation a été précédée par la caravane « Sunu Joj Sunu Gox », qui est allée à la rencontre des municipalités et des jeunes. C’est dans cette dynamique que s’inscrit le « Quartier général des Joj territorialisées », installé sur le terrain sportif de l’Unité 9 de Jaxaay-Parcelles et lancé ce mardi 3 novembre 2026. Pendant près de deux semaines, il accueillera des tournois de football masculin et féminin, des démonstrations d’arts martiaux, des compétitions de pétanque et des jeux de l’esprit, ainsi que des animations culturelles quotidiennes. Dalifort, Yeumbeul Sud et Nord, Jaxaay-Parcelles, Keur Massar Nord et Sud, Djiddah Thiaroye Kao, Médina Gounass, Wakhinane-Nimzatt, Sangalkam et Tivaouane Peulh-Niaga figurent parmi les communes partenaires. Des expositions sur les projets de l’Adm et des rencontres avec les médias sont également prévues. À travers cette initiative, l’Adm et le Cojoj ambitionnent de faire des Joj « Dakar 2026 » un levier de mobilisation de la jeunesse, de valorisation des territoires et de développement durable. Par Samba Oumar FALL

Orpailleurs burkinabè refoulés de Guinée : Une délégation gouvernementale à Bamako pour organiser leur retour au pays
items.description: Le Burkina Faso et le Mali se mobilisent pour faciliter le retour de plusieurs jeunes orpailleurs burkinabè refoulés de la République de Guinée. Dans cette perspective, le ministre burkinabè de la Sécurité, le commissaire divisionnaire de police Mahamadou Sana, et sa collègue de l'action humanitaire, Passowendé Pélagie Kabré/Kaboré, ont effectué une visite à Bamako, ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, à la tête d'une importante délégation. L'information est donnée par la Direction de l'information des relations publiques (DIRPA) des Forces armées maliennes (FAMA). À leur arrivée dans la capitale malienne, les deux ministres burkinabè ont été reçus en audience par leur homologue, le ministre malien de la Sécurité et de la Protection civile, le général de division Daoud Aly Mohammedine. Cette rencontre, selon la DIRPA, visait notamment à faire le point sur la situation des jeunes Burkinabè arrivés sur le territoire malien après avoir été refoulés de Guinée. Les trois personnalités ont également échangé sur les dispositions à prendre pour renforcer leur prise en charge et faciliter leur retour au Burkina Faso dans des conditions dignes et sécurisées. Mandatés par le président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, Mahamadou Sana et Passowendé Pélagie Kabré/Kaboré sont allés porter la préoccupation des plus hautes autorités burkinabè face à la situation de ces ressortissants. Les échanges ont ainsi permis d'examiner les mesures d'assistance à mettre en œuvre afin de favoriser leur retour auprès de leurs familles. À cette occasion, le ministre burkinabè de la Sécurité a salué l'hospitalité du peuple malien et exprimé la reconnaissance des autorités de son pays envers la République sœur du Mali pour l'accueil et l'accompagnement réservés à leurs compatriotes. Il a, par ailleurs, assuré que les autorités burkinabè, en étroite collaboration avec leurs homologues maliens, restent mobilisées pour apporter l'assistance nécessaire aux personnes concernées et faciliter leur rapatriement. Cette démarche s'inscrit dans le cadre de la coopération entre les deux pays, membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES). Elle met en avant les principes de solidarité, de fraternité et d'assistance mutuelle entre les États confédérés. Minute.bf

items.title: Silicon Valley’s Very Bad Night
items.description: For years, public anxiety and frustration over AI have been mounting. More than 80 percent of Americans think the technology is moving too quickly , and more than 70 percent oppose data-center construction in their area. Meanwhile, tech companies have spent hundreds of millions of dollars on this election to combat regulations and candidates they deem a threat. Yesterday, months of skirmishes between these two political forces culminated, for the first time, in a nationwide contest. All over the country, Silicon Valley was on the ballot. And for the most part, Silicon Valley lost. Residents of at least 10 states voted on dozens of proposals to restrict data-center development—local moratoriums, new zoning regulations—and several towns recalled mayors accused of putting the interests of data-center companies over those of constituents. Democratic candidates in some of the most consequential Senate races, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Sherrod Brown in Ohio, made AI and data-center regulation central to their campaigns. In California, the home of Silicon Valley, residents voted on a proposed “billionaire tax” that tech executives came out in droves to oppose. [ Read: The data-center rebellion is just beginning ] Again and again, Americans repudiated the AI boom and Silicon Valley, while candidates who made a point of blasting the tech companies won easily. Dozens of bans and restrictions on data-center development sailed through at the local level, and at least nine governors who support a statewide data-center ban will be in office next year. “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction,” Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia declared in his victory speech. His job, he said, will be to bring “Big Tech to heel.” For a quarter century, tech companies have been able to marshal capital and connections to beat back meaningful regulation with relative ease. In 2024, crypto spent more than $100 million to crush a slate of candidates, including Brown, then a three-time incumbent. But such wealth and influence have perhaps grown too great—yesterday’s results show that reining in Silicon Valley is now an urgent and galvanizing issue in our politics. Although federal regulation seems unlikely under a Trump presidency, towns in Ohio, Illinois, Kansas, Florida, and elsewhere passed anti-data-center measures, including temporarily banning or advising city governments to ban new data-center construction. More than 30 of these referenda passed, in red and blue counties alike; only one so far, to my knowledge, failed, in North Dakota. And at least three mayors, in Oklahoma and Ohio, were recalled for their prominent support of local data-center projects. (As Elon Musk posted on X last night, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”) Meanwhile, the candidates who ran on strong AI-regulation platforms swept the night. Less than a month before the election, El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, launched a plan to get “AI Under Control” and made the technology central to the final stretch of his campaign. “This is the existential crisis of our time,” El-Sayed told The New York Times . In Ohio, Brown put tech regulation front and center in his campaign while erecting billboards that painted his opponent as the “face of data centers.” Elsewhere, Gina Hinojosa crushed Greg Abbott in the race for governor of Texas in part by criticizing his support of—and late, unconvincing flip-flop on—data centers. New York Governor Kathy Hochul, after passing the first statewide data-center moratorium, won reelection with ease. In Pennsylvania, Democrats harped on data centers to flip four seats and take control of the state Senate for the first time in decades. Just how much weight AI carried in many of these victories is hard to ascertain, of course. The technology was the top issue for less than 1 percent of voters in a September New York Times poll. Inflation, the war in Iran, and the flaws of individual nominees likely played much larger roles than AI for many people; many of the candidates who won and were harshest on tech were also Democrats benefiting from outrage at Trump’s presidency. But another reason it’s hard to discern how data-center sentiment shifted votes is because of how popular data-center skepticism has become over the past year, both on the left and on the right. Ohio’s Jon Husted and Michigan’s Mike Rogers are two of many Republicans who tried to distance themselves from the data-center industry. These victories for critics of AI and data centers (and crypto, too ) are part of a broader shift against Silicon Valley over the past half decade. There’s a global techlash under way: Antitrust investigations in the U.S., strict privacy regulations in Europe, social-media lawsuits and bans around the world. Still, for the most part, Silicon Valley has been able to use its wealth and influence to beat back any substantive opponents or regulations in the U.S. This week, that playbook failed. Tech companies and executives poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Trump’s super PAC, inauguration fund, ballroom renovation, and other pet projects. Crypto and AI super PACs have spent still more, some $250 million, on this year’s federal elections, while Elon Musk alone has poured close to half a billion dollars into the midterms. Many of the candidates they spent the most on in competitive races lost; that use of wealth to buy power may be exactly what Americans voted against. The success of various anti-data-center ballot measures and candidates can be understood as a repudiation of Silicon Valley as much as one of the White House. The president has given both crypto and AI his blessing, and recently launched something of a pro-data-center tour, writing on Truth Social that the only reason communities “should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” (Many of the data-center moratoriums were passed in counties that voted for Trump in double digits in 2024.) But the proposal that most explicitly challenged Silicon Valley’s wealth—a literal wealth tax on billionaires proposed in California—appears poised for defeat. The measure, called Proposition 40, would have been a onetime tax on billionaires’ wealth to make up for cuts to the state’s health-care program in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Tech investors and entrepreneurs, many of them billionaires, donated more than $300 million to defeat the measure, framing it as an existential threat to the state’s start-up ecosystem. Still, that a wealth tax came close to passing at all—and until a recent adversarial blitz polled favorably —in the state home to, and traditionally proud of, an industry built on the promise of amassing wealth is itself indicative of the most fundamental concern underlying the techlash. Even before yesterday’s election, Silicon Valley was fretting about 2028. Tech firms have been clamoring to get Democratic consultants on the phone and coming up with all manner of ideas to quell the data-center backlash. OpenAI’s head lobbyist, Chris Lehane, has been reportedly circulating a memo among lawmakers in Washington predicting that AI will be a defining issue of the 2028 election. The memo, obtained by Politico , begins, “We already know the number-one issue of the 2028 presidential election: AI. What we don’t know is how it will show up.” Tuesday’s results suggest otherwise.

items.title: School is your biggest networking opportunity; make the most of it – MC Kabutey
items.description: Ghanaian event host MC Kabutey has urged students to look beyond academic work and take advantage of the relationships and experiences available to them while in school, saying these could open doors to opportunities later in life. Speaking on The Career Trail Season 4 on Joy Learning TV and Joy News, he encouraged young people to meet new people, explore unfamiliar interests and make themselves known within their school communities. Sharing his experience at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), he recalled deciding to spend his first year exploring the different activities and communities on campus. One of his discoveries was the Campus Christian Family (CCF), where students from different academic backgrounds came together to stage drama performances based on Bible stories before Sunday sermons. He said he was fascinated by the acting, costumes and creativity that went into the productions, which inspired him to join the Communication Arts Department (CAD) when he returned for his second semester. “That was the beginning of my theatre, acting and emceeing life. I discovered theatre, I discovered acting. And I just did it for fun because I just loved it, I was just excited about it,” he recounted. His involvement in the department also introduced him to people who would later occupy significant positions in their respective fields. Among them was the current Minister of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, who was his colleague in the university’s mass drama group. “Somebody like Honourable Samuel George was my colleague in mass drama. He was technical director, I was drama director. Today he’s a Minister of Communications, he’s a Member of Parliament,” he said. MC Kabutey also recounted how his interest in exploring new experiences led him to salsa dancing while at KNUST. Although some members of the Christian community had reservations about the dance style, he said he was curious to learn it and eventually joined a salsa group at Independence Hall. He continued dancing at the Aviation Social Centre after leaving university, where he met people including Chatterhouse Public Relations Officer, Robert Klah. He said these experiences showed him how participating in activities outside the classroom could introduce young people to new communities and relationships they might never have encountered otherwise. He also argued that simply knowing a prominent person does not necessarily translate into opportunities, but a relationship in which that person knows you and recognises your value could make a difference. “Who you know is a good thing. If you know a big person, if you know an influential person, it’s a good thing. But do you know what is even better than whom you know? It’s who knows you,” he said. “As you and I sit here, we know President Mahama, right? What has your knowing President Mahama done for your life? No. But the day President Mahama gets to know you like the way he knows me; that is the big deal. You know I was honored to host his 30th wedding anniversary and to host a few state events. He knows me and I know him,” he added. Mc Kabutey urged students to see their time in secondary school and university as an important opportunity to build lasting relationships. “The university, the secondary school, is the biggest, is your final mass congregation space you will ever be in. For the rest of your life, you will likely never, ever be confined in a space that has that many people at the same time,” he echoed.

items.title: Détournement présumé de 3 tonnes d’or à la BCRG : Karamo Kaba, Abdoulaye Yéro Baldé et autres cités à comparaître le 23 novembre
items.description: Le procès dans l’affaire du détournement présumé de trois tonnes d’or à la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG) s’est ouvert ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 devant la chambre de jugement de la Cour de répression des infractions économiques et financières (CRIEF). À l’issue de l’audience, la comparution de quatre personnalités a été ordonnée pour le 23 novembre prochain. Il s’agit de l’actuel gouverneur de la BCRG, Karamo Kaba, de l’ancien vice-gouverneur Abdoulaye Yéro Baldé, du directeur juridique de la Banque centrale, Daouda Diané, et de Mamady Condé, représentant de la société Affinor en Guinée. Cette procédure met en cause l’ancien gouverneur de la BCRG sous le régime déchu, Dr Lounceny Nabé. Il est poursuivi pour le détournement présumé de 3 tonnes et 135 kilogrammes d’or destinés à la société Affinor, basée en Belgique, dans le cadre d’un contrat signé en 2015 portant sur l’affinage et la gestion d’une partie des réserves d’or de la République de Guinée. Des accusations que l’ancien patron de la Banque centrale rejette catégoriquement. À la barre, il a soutenu que les trois tonnes d’or, évaluées à environ 200 millions de dollars, se trouvent toujours entre les mains de la société Affinor. « Je ne reconnais pas les faits. C’est Affinor qui détient les trois tonnes d’or. Je n’ai aucun lien personnel avec eux. Cela me blesse que les gens pensent que j’ai détourné trois tonnes d’or. D’ailleurs, il y a eu une bataille de procédure dans cette affaire entre la Guinée et Affinor, et la Guinée l’a remportée. Par conséquent, je pense qu’on ne peut plus parler de détournement », a déclaré l’ancien gouverneur. Dans le souci de faire toute la lumière sur cette affaire, le parquet spécial, représenté par le procureur Biwon Millimono, a sollicité la comparution de Mamady Condé, représentant d’Affinor en Guinée, ainsi que celle d’Abdoulaye Yéro Baldé, ancien vice-gouverneur, et de l’actuel gouverneur de la BCRG, Karamo Kaba. De son côté, la défense a également demandé l’audition de Daouda Diané, directeur juridique de la Banque centrale, présenté comme le responsable de l’élaboration du contrat au cœur de cette procédure. Après avoir entendu les différentes parties, la cour a ordonné la comparution des quatre personnes citées en qualité de témoins et renvoyé l’affaire au 23 novembre 2026. Elisa Camara L’article Détournement présumé de 3 tonnes d’or à la BCRG : Karamo Kaba, Abdoulaye Yéro Baldé et autres cités à comparaître le 23 novembre est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Big money flops as Democrats sweep US Congress
items.description: Hundreds of millions of dollars spent, with little to show for it. The rout of President Donald Trump and his Republicans in the US midterm elections was also a defeat for Elon Musk and for the massive campaign spending meant to sway voters. Democrats captured both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday in a stunning rejection of Trump’s political agenda, winning races in which conservative groups had poured in far more outside money than their liberal counterparts. “This might have been the biggest defeat for big money in American political history,” Logan Phillips, founder of the election forecasting site Race to the White House, wrote on X. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk said on X, with a shrug emoji. Musk contributed nearly half a billion dollars to Republican efforts, making him the largest individual contributor in a federal election cycle since 2010, according to campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets. That year, the Supreme Court ruled that the government cannot limit political spending by corporations, unions and other groups acting independently of candidates, opening the way for big donors to pour vast sums into elections, sometimes anonymously. ‘Our own Goliaths’ More than $200 million of Musk’s money went to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas. Democrat James Talarico defeated Paxton, a close Trump ally, to become the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994. “In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire Washington, DC establishment,” Talarico said. He also targeted billionaires “who own the social media algorithms, who own the cable news networks, who own the politicians fighting on our screens” and who “want us at each other’s throats”. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown unseated Republican Senator Jon Husted in the country’s second most expensive race, with more than $500m spent. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson in the governor’s race, after he poured more than $200m of his fortune into his bid, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution . In Ohio, biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy lost the governor’s race to Democrat Amy Acton after putting an estimated $36m of his own money into it. AI industry money also fell short. In South Carolina, American Mission, the Republican arm of the Leading the Future network backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, put about $2.7m behind Senator Darline Graham, who lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in a state Trump won by 18 points. Building the Future, a new data centre industry super PAC tied to Leading the Future, had made Graham its first candidate to back. ‘Cannot yield’ Democrats also had billionaire backing. Former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg spent $80m on House, Senate and governor races, then added $36m in the final days, Politico reported. Bloomberg’s political adviser Howard Wolfson told CNN that “money is not determinative, but it is helpful”, noting that Republicans held a significant financial advantage. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, who put $11.5m into the super PAC backing Talarico, said “we should get money out of politics”. “And while people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield,” Hoffman wrote on X late on Tuesday, defending his largesse. In California, a ballot proposal for a one-time five per cent tax on the state’s billionaires seemed to have failed after some of its wealthiest residents spent hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat it.

Petrol price dropped by Rs7.06 per litre, high-speed diesel by Rs3.71
items.description: The government on Wednesday cut the price of petrol by Rs7.06 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.71. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs362.00 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs387.81 on Nov 5 (Thursday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). Wednesday’s cut is the third consecutive reduction in fuel prices. It came as international oil prices fell under $100 in volatile trade on Wednesday, with investors awaiting Washington’s next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections. Brent futures were down $4.50, or 4.3 per cent, to $99.07 a barrel at 1619 GMT (9:19pm, PKT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures are down $4.13, or 4.3pc, to $92.02. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Meanwhile, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the government are set to follow up on their recent discussions on possible relief in petroleum prices and hold another round of talks on Thursday, the party said. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene. Additional input by Reuters

items.title: ECOM Ghana commissions new school facilities at Konkoma, charges farmers to safeguard cocoa farms
items.description: Management of ECOM Ghana and Sustainable Management Services is distraught over the growing trend of cocoa farmers leasing their plantations and lands for illegal mining operations. The leading private licensed cocoa buying company (LBC) and agricultural services group observes that a significant number of farmers are selling out their lands for immediate profits. According to ECOM Ghana, the trend threatens the sustainability of the cocoa industry as the practice continues to destroy livelihoods, farmlands and the future of cocoa-growing communities. Acting General Manager of Sustainability at ECOM Ghana, Emmanuel Baffoe-Bonnie expressed the concern during the handing over of a three-unit classroom block and other ancillary facilities to the Konkoma D/A Basic School in the Ashanti Region. He noted that while the company continues to invest in schools, water, and other social infrastructure to improve lives in cocoa-growing communities, some farmers are giving up their farms for short-term gains from illegal mining. He pleaded with the farmers to resist any enticement to sell their farms for illegal mining activities. “I appeal to cocoa farmers not to sell their cocoa farms to illegal miners. It is true that illegal mining can bring quick money, but it is not sustainable. We must think beyond today. We must think about our children and our grandchildren. We must also think about the environment, the water bodies in our communities, and look beyond money,” he said. Mr. Baffoe-Bonnie said the activities are eroding the foundation of rural prosperity, urging farmers to protect their farms, safeguard the environment, and preserve the cocoa heritage for future generations. “What negative impact are we experiencing from illegal mining in our communities? Farmers should therefore continue to engage in cocoa farming. They should put in the effort to practise good agricultural, environmental and social practices to ensure that cocoa is maintained and becomes sustainable,” he added. ECOM Ghana and its partners, Ferrero, also handed over a four-seater toilet facility, recycled dual desks, and teaching and learning materials to the school located in the Bosomtwe district. Headmaster of Konkoma D/A Basic School, Nana Yaw Kwakye-Adeefe, recounted the unpleasant and challenging conditions the school endured prior to the construction of the new classroom block. He explained that a horde of the students were compelled to have lessons in a makeshift wooden structure, while others contended for the only four permanent classrooms at the school. According to him, learning under the open structure was a constant struggle as rain often disrupted lessons, and dust from untarred roads close to the school choked students. “We deeply appreciate ECOM Ghana and its partners for coming to the school’s aid, as the new facilities will go a long way to improve teaching, learning and sanitation in the school,” he said. The new facilities are intended to create a more conducive environment for teaching and learning, improve access to sanitation and contribute to the general well-being of both pupils and teachers. “These investments reflect our firm belief that access to clean water and quality education are fundamental to building healthy, resilient and prosperous communities,” Mr. Baffoe-Bonnie said. The Konkoma project forms part of ECOM Ghana’s vision of Creating Rural Prosperity, demonstrating its commitments to rural development and to improving teaching and learning in cocoa-growing communities. Over the years, the company has provided more than 400 potable water sources to improve access to safe drinking water and constructed over 50 school blocks to support teaching and learning in communities across its operational areas. Business Head of ECOM Ghana, Richard Suwli, urged the school authorities, teachers, pupils, parents and the community members to take ownership of the facilities. He charged them to ensure their proper maintenance, responsible utilisation and preservation for the benefit of posterity. “The true value of any development intervention lies not merely in its construction or provision, but in the positive and lasting impact it creates in people’s lives,” he said. He expressed profound appreciation to Ferrero for its partnership, noting that it had played an instrumental role in actualizing the project. Meanwhile, Asokwa Municipal Director of Education, Reverend Ebenezer Oteng Marfo, assured stakeholders of the meticulous safeguarding of the facilities, highlighting how they intend to properly maintain them.

items.title: El papa León XIV recibe a Bob Dylan en el Vaticano

items.title: Police Service cautions motorists against fake traffic fine messages under Traffitech-GH
items.description: The Ghana Police Service has cautioned motorists and vehicle owners against fraudulent traffic fine notifications, following the official commencement of the Traffitech-GH automated traffic enforcement project on November 1, 2026. In a statement on Wednesday, November 4, the Police said the initiative, which seeks to automate the enforcement of road traffic laws and regulations, requires motorists to observe approved procedures for verifying and paying traffic fines. The Service advised motorists to first check that traffic violation notifications come from the official sender ID, GPS-MTTD, warning that genuine notifications would not be sent from ordinary mobile phone numbers. It also urged recipients to open their Electronic Notice of Violation (ENV) or traffic ticket to verify the vehicle photograph and registration number, as well as the location, date and time of the alleged offence. Motorists were further encouraged to watch the accompanying video where available. According to the Police, traffic fines can be paid through the National Investment Bank (NIB) Payment Portal or a USSD platform. To make payments online, motorists are required to visit the traffictech website, select the ‘Make Payment’ option, enter their ticket number, verify the details and follow the payment instructions. Alternatively, they can dial *710*0# and follow the prompts to make a payment using their ticket number. The Police particularly warned motorists against paying traffic fines into personal mobile money numbers or through unofficial accounts, urging the public to remain vigilant to avoid falling victim to fraud. For assistance or further enquiries, the statement said motorists can contact the Ghana Police Service on 0596922402. The Service expressed appreciation to motorists, vehicle owners and transport operators for their cooperation and support in promoting road safety and compliance with traffic regulations.
